title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
會試錄序
聖天子龍飛紀元嘉靖之二年歲
在癸未將
親策天下貢士於廷
詔禮部舉行會試之典試士之
期例以辰戌丑未之年前此
兩癸未初為永樂元年後為
===
天順八年皆不果如例自有
定制以來惟今年癸未始如期
而試
天眷
聖明將益昌文運復
祖宗渾厚淳古之風於今日可由
此而預卜矣豈不足為世道

會試錄序

聖天子龍飛紀元嘉靖之二年，歲在癸未，將親策天下貢士於廷，詔禮部舉行會試之典。試士之期，例以辰戌丑未之年。前此兩癸未，初為永樂元年，後為天順八年，皆不果如例。自有定制以來，惟今年癸未始如期而試。天眷聖明，將益昌文運，復祖宗渾厚淳古之風於今日，可由此而預卜矣。豈不足為世道
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

In the second year of Jiajing, the reign inaugurated upon the sagely Son of Heaven’s accession, the year guiwei, he was preparing personally to examine the tribute scholars from throughout the realm with policy questions at court. He commanded the Ministry of Rites to conduct the Metropolitan Examination. By established practice, examinations of scholars are held in years bearing the earthly branches chen, xu, chou, and wei. Of the two preceding guiwei years, the first was the first year of Yongle and the latter the eighth year of Tianshun [?]. In neither case was the examination actually held according to established practice. Since the regular system was established, only in this guiwei year has the examination first been held as scheduled.

Heaven favors our sagely and enlightened sovereign: literary achievement will flourish still further, and the generous, sincere, and unadorned ways of the imperial ancestors will be restored in our own day. From this event we may already foresee it. Is this not sufficient cause for the moral order of the age to …

同考試則修撰臣呂柟臣楊
慎編修臣王思臣黃初臣葉
式臣陳沂臣江暉臣馬汝驥臣

劉儲秀主事臣薛蕙臣唐冑監
試則御史臣唐鳳儀臣牛天麟暨

其文於三千六百卷中恭從

His Majesty commanded your servants Jiang Mian and Shi Bao to take charge of rejecting and selecting candidates. The Associate Examiners were your servants Lü Nan and Yang Shen, Senior Compilers; Wang Si, Huang Chu, Ye Shi, Chen Yi, Jiang Hui, Ma Ruji, Sun Yuan, and Huang Zuo, Junior Compilers; Lin Shi, Examining Editor; Zhang Chong, Left Supervising Secretary; Xia Yan and Zhao Tingrui, Supervising Secretaries; Liu Chuxiu, Secretary acting as Director; and Xue Hui and Tang Zhou, Secretaries. title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
武乙丑永樂甲申兩科之外
僅再見焉於戲盛矣爰刻其
氏名及文為會試錄既成臣
冕謹序其首竊惟文運與氣
運相為流通未有氣運方盛
而文運不亨者也特在乎斡
旋轉移之有其道耳操斡旋
===
轉移之柄非有賴於位隆
君師身任斯文之責者歟我
國家稽古設科以文取士而用
之用其人矣而尤資其文以
為世用用之
朝廷用之天下不可一日無也
是故輔養

君師身任斯文之責者歟我
國家稽古設科以文取士而用
之用其人矣而尤資其文以
爲世用用之
朝廷用之天下不可一日無也
是故輔養
punctuated:
武乙丑、永樂甲申兩科之外，僅再見焉。於戲，盛矣！爰刻其氏名及文，為《會試錄》。既成，臣冕謹序其首。
竊惟文運與氣運相為流通，未有氣運方盛而文運不亨者也。特在乎斡旋轉移之有其道耳。操斡旋轉移之柄，非有賴於位隆君師、身任斯文之責者歟？我國家稽古設科，以文取士而用之。用其人矣，而尤資其文以為世用。用之朝廷，用之天下，不可一日無也。是故輔養
translation_en:
…apart from the two examinations held in the yichou year of the Hongwu reign and the jiashen year of the Yongle reign, such numbers have only now been seen again. Ah, how flourishing! Accordingly, the candidates’ names and their compositions were engraved for printing as the Record of the Metropolitan Examination. Once it was completed, I, your servant Mian, respectfully wrote this preface for its opening.
I humbly consider that the fortunes of literary culture and the currents of the age flow into and through one another. Never have the currents of the age been flourishing while literary culture failed to prosper. It depends only upon having the proper means of guiding and redirecting them. Does not wielding the power to guide and redirect them depend upon one who occupies the exalted position of ruler and teacher and personally bears responsibility for this literary culture? Our dynasty, consulting antiquity, established the examinations to select men through their writing and employ them. It employs the men themselves, but relies especially upon their writing for service to the world. Such writing is used at court and throughout the realm; not a single day can pass without it. Thus, for nurturing and fostering…

text:

經筵紀載

國史祭饗

格

德意别是非以不惑乎
聖聰明予奪以求定乎國是若此
者非文無以適於用也以至
銓衡人物出納財賦申明典

君心昭鑒戒感通神明宣布
德意別是非以不惑乎
聖聰明予奪以求定乎國是若此
者非文無以適於用也以至
銓衡人物出納財賦申明典
章修和禮樂陳師鞠旅明罰
勑法君工虞振紀綱諸大政
punctuated: 德義則有經筵，紀載謨烈則有國史，祭饗郊廟則有祠祝，播告寰宇則有詔令，獻替可否則有章疏，所以格君心、昭鑒戒、感通神明、宣布德意、别是非以不惑乎聖聰、明予奪以求定乎國是。若此者，非文無以適於用也。以至銓衡人物、出納財賦、申明典章、修和禮樂、陳師鞠旅、明罰勑法、若工虞、振紀綱，諸大政
translation_en: …virtue and righteousness, there are the Classics Colloquia; to record imperial counsels and achievements, there is the dynastic history; for sacrifices at the suburban altars and ancestral temples, there are sacrificial prayers; to issue proclamations throughout the realm, there are edicts and commands; to recommend what is acceptable and oppose what is not, there are memorials. These serve to rectify the ruler’s mind, make lessons and warnings clear, communicate with the spirits, proclaim the ruler’s benevolent intentions, distinguish right from wrong so that the imperial understanding is not confused, and clarify the granting and withholding of rewards and recognition so as to establish a settled course of state policy. In such matters, without literary composition there is no means of meeting practical needs. This extends to assessing and selecting men, receiving and disbursing revenues, elucidating statutes and institutions, cultivating and harmonizing rites and music, deploying armies and mustering troops, making punishments clear and enforcing laws, directing the offices of works and forestry [?], and strengthening the framework of governance—all these great affairs of state…

title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
外而旬宣糾察於藩臬撫綏
勞来於郡邑莫不各有當然
之則與其已然之故必欲一
一循理奉法敷陳於上訓諭
於下粲然有文以相經緯而
後行無不達顧一於科目焉
取之科試之文其切於世用
===
蓋如此或者乃謂其無關世
道豈識達治體之論哉
聖天子誕膺景運方將丕闡人文
以化成天下驅澆漓詭異之
習以為渾厚淳古之歸以復
我
祖宗之舊言行政事無偏無黨咸

外而旬宣糾察於藩臬亦撫綏
勞來於郡邑莫不各有當然
之則與其已然之故必欲一
一循理奉法敷陳於上訓諭
於下翼然有文以相經緯而
後行無不違顧一於科目焉
取之科試之文其切於世用
盖如此或者乃謂其無關世
道豈識達治體之論哉
===
聖天子誕膺景運方將丕闡人文
以化成天下驅澆漓詭異之
習以為渾厚淳古之歸以復
我
祖宗之舊言行政事無偏無黨成
punctuated:
外而旬宣糾察於藩臬，撫綏勞来於郡邑，莫不各有當然之則與其已然之故。必欲一一循理奉法，敷陳於上，訓諭於下，粲然有文以相經緯，而後行無不達。顧一於科目焉取之，科試之文，其切於世用蓋如此。或者乃謂其無關世道，豈識達治體之論哉？
聖天子誕膺景運，方將丕闡人文，以化成天下，驅澆漓詭異之習，以為渾厚淳古之歸，以復我祖宗之舊。言行政事，無偏無黨，咸
translation_en:
…and outside the capital, in conducting regional tours of inspection and scrutiny through the provincial administration and surveillance commissions, and in pacifying and comforting the people in prefectures and counties, every undertaking has its proper governing principles and the reasons behind its existing circumstances. In every instance, officials must follow principle and uphold the law, presenting matters to their superiors and instructing those below. Only when lucid writing gives these activities an interconnected order can their execution proceed without impediment. Yet it is exclusively through the examinations that such men are recruited. Such, then, is the practical relevance of examination writing to the affairs of the world. Some nevertheless claim that it has no bearing on the moral and political order. Can this be the judgment of anyone who understands the essentials of governance?
Our sagely Son of Heaven has received the mandate of an auspicious age and is now about to bring human culture to full flourishing, thereby transforming and perfecting all under Heaven. He will turn shallow, insincere, and aberrant habits toward substantial virtue and ancient simplicity, restoring the old ways of our imperial ancestors. In speech, conduct, and affairs of government, without partiality or faction, all …

title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
躋之正大光明之域盖不獨
科試一事為然而機括轉移
則實自科試始
聖意所嚮天下之士孰不曉然不
假乎
渙汗之申嚴
張操縱間一
===
已昌遂有
天心之允協振
德教於安□
以垂法萬世氣運已盛而益
盛
國運已延而益延其兆具見於
今日人皆知其有必然者

punctuated: 躋之正大光明之域。盖不獨科試一事為然，而機括轉移，則實自科試始。聖意所嚮，天下之士孰不曉然？不假乎渙汗之申嚴。張操縱間，一已昌遂有天心之允協，振德教於安□，以垂法萬世。氣運已盛而益盛，國運已延而益延，其兆具見於今日，人皆知其有必然者。
translation_en: …bring them into the realm of rectitude and openness. This is not true of the examinations alone; yet the decisive change does indeed begin with the examinations. Who among the scholars of the realm does not clearly understand the direction of the imperial will, without needing solemn reiterations through imperial proclamations? In the exercise of control [?], flourishing has already come about [?], with Heaven’s will in full accord. Moral instruction is invigorated amid peace [illegible character; sense uncertain], establishing a model for ten thousand generations. The prevailing fortunes, already flourishing, will flourish still more; the dynasty’s fortunes, already prolonged, will be prolonged still further. The signs of this are all visible today, and everyone knows that it is certain to come about.

title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
聖神功化不疾而速固如是夫凡
生斯世際斯會者皆將感奮
踴躍更相慶幸而況登名是
錄獲以其文用世者哉詩不
云乎無言□
諸士其將
上哉
===
光祿大夫□
太傅戶部
士蔣冕謹序

主斯世際斯會者皆將感奮
踴躍更相慶幸而况登名是
錄獲以其文用世者哉詩不

光祿大夫上
太傅戶部
士蔣冕謹序
punctuated:
聖神功化，不疾而速，固如是夫！凡生斯世、際斯會者，皆將感奮踴躍，更相慶幸，而況登名是錄，獲以其文用世者哉！詩不云乎：「無言□。」諸士其將上哉！

光祿大夫□太傅戶部士蔣冕謹序。
translation_en:
…The achievements and transforming influence of sagely, divine rule are swift without haste: surely this is so! All who live in this age and encounter this occasion will be moved to eager enthusiasm and congratulate one another on their good fortune. How much more so those whose names appear in this record and who gain the opportunity to serve the world through their literary accomplishments! Does not the Book of Odes say, “Without words □” [?]? May you gentlemen advance [?]!

Jiang Mian, Grand Master for Splendid Happiness, □ Grand Preceptor, Ministry of Revenue [remainder of title garbled: 士], respectfully composed this preface.

translation_en:
Metropolitan Examination of the Second Year of Jiajing (1523)

Officials in Charge of the Examination

Mao Cheng, Grand Master for Aid in Governance and Minister of Rites, had the courtesy name Xianqing. He was from Taicang Subprefecture in Zhili and became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in the guichou year.

Jia Yong, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Left Vice Minister of Rites, had the courtesy name Minghe. He was from Linying County in Henan and became a metropolitan graduate in the bingchen year.

Examiners

Jiang Mian, Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, Pillar of State, Junior Preceptor concurrently serving as Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent, Minister of Revenue, and Grand Secretary of the Jinshen Hall, had the courtesy name Jingzhi. He was from Quanzhou in Guangxi and became a metropolitan graduate in the dingwei year.

Shi Bao, Grand Master for Fostering Goodness and Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent concurrently serving as Academician of the Hanlin Academy, had the courtesy name Bangyan. He was from Gaocheng County in Zhili and became a metropolitan graduate in the dingwei year.

Associate Examiners

Lü Nan, Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Scholarly Service, had the courtesy name Zhongmu. He was from Gaoling County in Shaanxi and became a metropolitan graduate in the wuchen year.

Yang Weicong, Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Scholarly Service, had the courtesy name Dafu. He was from Gu'an County in Shuntian Prefecture and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinsi year.

Wang Si, Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, had the courtesy name Yixue. He was from Taihe County in Jiangxi and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinwei year.

Huang Chu, Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Literary Service, had the courtesy name Shenqing. He was from Guixi County in Jiangxi and became a metropolitan graduate in the jiaxu year.

Ye Shi, Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Literary Service, had the courtesy name Chenggui. He was from Yongjia County in Zhejiang and became a metropolitan graduate in the dingchou year.

Chen Yi, Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Literary Service, had the courtesy name Lunan. His household was registered with the Imperial Medical Office in Nanjing; he was from Yin County in Zhejiang and became a metropolitan graduate in the dingchou year.

Jiang Hui, Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Literary Service, had the courtesy name Jingfu. He was from Renhe County in Zhejiang and became a metropolitan graduate in the dingchou year.

Ma Ruji, Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Literary Service, had the courtesy name Zhongfang. He was from Suide Subprefecture in Shaanxi and became a metropolitan graduate in the dingchou year.

Sun Yuan, Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Literary Service, had the courtesy name Congyi. He was from Anlu Subprefecture in Huguang and became a metropolitan graduate in the jiaxu year.

Fei Cai, Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, had the courtesy name Zichong. He was from Yanshan County in Jiangxi and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinsi year.

translation_en:
Lin Shi, courtesy name Maoyi, was an Examining Editor in the Hanlin Academy, holding the prestige title Zhengshilang. He was from Ruyang County, Henan, and became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in the dingchou year (1517).

Zhang Chong, courtesy name Xizhi, was Left Supervising Secretary in the Office of Scrutiny for Justice, holding the prestige title Zhengshilang. He was from Tongchuan Subprefecture, Sichuan, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinwei year (1511).

Xia Yan, courtesy name Gongjin, was a Supervising Secretary in the Office of Scrutiny for Military Affairs, holding the prestige title Zhengshilang. He was from Guixi County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the dingchou year (1517).

Zhao Tingrui, courtesy name Xinchen, was a Supervising Secretary in the Office of Scrutiny for Revenue. He was from Kai Subprefecture, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinsi year (1521).

Liu Chuxiu, courtesy name Shiqi, was a Secretary serving as acting Director of the Huguang Bureau in the Ministry of Justice, holding the prestige title Chengdelang. He was from Xianning County, Shaanxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the jiaxu year (1514).

Xue Hui, courtesy name Juncai, was a Secretary in the Bureau of Personnel Appointments in the Ministry of Personnel, holding the prestige title Chengdelang. He was registered with Wuping Guard in Zhili, was a native of Yanshi County, Henan, and became a metropolitan graduate in the jiaxu year (1514).

Tang Zhou, courtesy name Pinghou, was a Secretary in the Guangxi Bureau of the Ministry of Revenue, holding the prestige title Chengdelang. He was from Qiongshan County, Guangdong, and became a metropolitan graduate in the renxu year (1502).

Examination Monitoring Officials:

Tang Fengyi, courtesy name Yingshao, was an Investigating Censor for the Henan Circuit, holding the prestige title Wenlinlang. He was from Shaoyang County, Huguang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the wuchen year (1508).

Niu Tianlin, courtesy name Wenxiang, was an Investigating Censor for the Yunnan Circuit, holding the prestige title Wenlinlang. He was from Liaocheng County, Shandong, and became a metropolitan graduate in the wuchen year (1508).

Proctors:

Wan Chao, courtesy name Ruxin, was a Secretary serving as acting Vice Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, holding the prestige title Chengdelang. He was from Jinxian County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinwei year (1511).

Zhang Can, courtesy name Jingchuan, was a Secretary in the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, holding the prestige title Chengdelang. He was from Shunde County, Guangdong, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinwei year (1511).

Officials Responsible for Printing Examination Papers:

Yu Cai, courtesy name Dezhong, was Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, holding the prestige title Fengzheng Dafu. He was from Neijiang County, Sichuan, and became a metropolitan graduate in the jiaxu year (1514).

Zhang Tang, courtesy name Tingjin, was a Secretary in the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites, holding the prestige title Chengdelang. He was from the jurisdiction of the Wanquan Regional Military Commission and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinwei year (1511).

Officials Responsible for Receiving and Keeping Examination Scripts:

Ma Tianyou, courtesy name Xichun, was a Central Drafting Office Secretary, holding the prestige title Zhengshilang. He was from Jun Subprefecture, Henan, and was a student admitted by virtue of official family status.

translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“The gentleman studies widely in the realm of letters and restrains himself through ritual; thus he may indeed avoid departing from the Way!”
“Above, he follows the patterns of Heaven’s seasons; below, he accords with the waters and the land.”
“As for the Way of Yao and Shun, without benevolent government one cannot bring peace and order to all under Heaven.”

Book of Changes

“Contemplation: the ritual washing has taken place, but the offering has not yet been presented. There is sincerity and a reverent bearing. Those below observe and are thereby transformed.”
“Nine in the fifth place: there is sincerity and a benevolent heart. Without needing to inquire, there is supreme good fortune. There is sincerity in reciprocating my virtue.”

…government, in [illegible]. At the imperial court, [illegible] and [illegible] are alike [?]; could one, together with [illegible] lords, undertake [illegible] [?]? [Illegible.] If, then, one wishes to accomplish [illegible] throughout all under Heaven, what is to be set right [?]? The Book of Odes says: “Give them guiding cords; give them ordering threads.” This refers to [illegible]. If you, sir, should participate in [illegible], issuing forth from the [illegible] of the vermilion screen behind the imperial throne [?]…

禮記
translation_en:
… said: “Resentment and lamentation—how difficult these are to deal with! Consider the difficulties in order to devise ways of easing them; then the people will be at peace.”

Book of Odes

The wings of the locusts—how thickly they gather! May your descendants flourish in great numbers!

Heaven protects and establishes you, granting you abundant goodness. Nothing fails to prosper; you receive Heaven’s hundred blessings. It sends down lasting blessings upon you, as though each day were too short to bestow them all.

Harmonious within the palace, reverent within the ancestral temple. Even when unseen, you are present; tirelessly you maintain your care.

The High God’s charge did not waver; with Tang it reached fulfilment. Tang’s coming was not delayed; his sagely reverence increased daily. His radiant influence reached far and endured [?]; he revered the High God. The High God’s charge became the rule throughout the nine regions.

Spring and Autumn Annals

The Di entered Wei. 〔Second year of Duke Min.〕 Chu Qiu was fortified. 〔Second year of Duke Xi.〕 Wu attacked Yue. 〔Thirty-second year of Duke Zhao.〕 Yuyue entered Wu. 〔Thirteenth year of Duke Ai.〕

The Duke and the Marquis of Qi arranged peace between Ju and Tan. The people of Ju refused to accept it. The Duke attacked Ju and captured Xiang. 〔Fourth year of Duke Xuan.〕

Shusun Qiaoru led an army to besiege Ji. 〔Third year of Duke Cheng.〕

The Son of Heaven sent the Earl of Shao to confer a patent of appointment upon the Duke. 〔Eighth year of Duke Cheng.〕 The Earl of Cao returned from the royal capital. 〔Sixteenth year of Duke Cheng.〕

Book of Rites

title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
大道之行也與三代之英丘未之逮也而
有志焉
夫民有血氣心知之性而無哀樂喜怒之
常應感起物而動然後心術形焉
恭儉莊敬而不煩則深於禮者也
可言也不可行君子弗言也可行也不可

大道之行也，與三代之英，丘未之逮也，而有志焉。
夫民有血氣心知之性，而無哀樂喜怒之常，應感起物而動，然後心術形焉。

translation_en:
“The practice of the Great Way and the outstanding figures of the Three Dynasties—I, Qiu, did not live to encounter them, but there are records of them.”
“The people possess the natural endowments of blood and vital energy, mind and understanding, yet their sorrow, pleasure, joy, and anger have no fixed constancy. They move in response to stimuli and external things [?], and only then do the workings of the mind become manifest.”
“One who is respectful, frugal, dignified, and reverent without being tiresome has a profound understanding of ritual.”
“What can be spoken of but cannot be put into practice, the gentleman does not speak of; what can be put into practice but cannot be spoken of, the gentleman does not practice.”
Second Session
Discourse
“The mind of the sage is one with Heaven.”
Imperial Proclamations, Commands, and Memorials of Thanks〔One question in this category [?]〕
Compose an imperial proclamation in the manner of the Han dynasty dispatching Grand Masters of Splendid Happiness to make inspection tours throughout the realm.
Compose an imperial command in the manner of the Tang dynasty appointing Wen Yanbo as Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs.
Compose a memorial of thanks in the manner of the Song dynasty for an imperial proclamation issued to the various prefectures enjoining compassion in the administration of punishments.
Legal Judgments〔Five items〕
Indiscriminately establishing posts for officials and clerks.
Households are to be determined by the registers.
Serving officials erecting stelae in their own honor without authorization.

title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
不操練軍士
有司官吏不住公廨
第叄場
策五道
問自三代而後不嗜殺人而一天下未有
如我
太祖高皇帝者也故方其初渡江至姑孰也有
進神武不殺之言者既從而善之及至
金陵有以不殺對所問者又從而喜之
他日自宣至徽厯舉漢高祖光武唐太
宗宋太祖四君所以取天下之道延問
故老一聞不嗜殺人之對則即
賜以衣帛慰諭再三不但善之喜之而已自
是以來凡攻取郡縣告諭群雄以至傳
檄遣將北定中原無一不以妄殺為戒
不數載而天下遂定於一矣然則人君
之一天下其道果不出於此歟宋儒蘇
氏嘗以此許前所稱四君矣不知四君

Question: Since the Three Dynasties, among those who have united All under Heaven without delighting in killing, none has equaled our Emperor Taizu Gao. Thus, when he first crossed the Yangzi and reached Gushu, someone offered the counsel that divine martial prowess does not kill; he accepted and approved it. Upon reaching Jinling, someone answered his inquiry by advising against killing; again he accepted the advice with pleasure. On another occasion, traveling from Xuan to Hui, he enumerated the ways in which the four rulers—Gaozu and Guangwu of the Han, Taizong of the Tang, and Taizu of the Song—had won All under Heaven, and invited local elders to discuss them. As soon as he heard the reply that they had taken no delight in killing, he bestowed clothing and silk, repeatedly offering words of reassurance and encouragement: he did more than merely approve and rejoice. From then onward, in capturing prefectures and counties, issuing proclamations to rival leaders, and even dispatching military proclamations and commanders to pacify the Central Plain in the north, he invariably warned against indiscriminate killing. Within a few years, All under Heaven was united and at peace. Is this, then, truly the whole of the way by which a ruler unites All under Heaven? The Song Confucian scholar Su once praised the four rulers named above on these grounds. We wonder whether these four rulers…

punctuated: 之事，亦有能彷彿我聖祖萬一者乎？無也。漢除秦莽之亂，唐除隋亂，宋除五季之亂，是四君者亦不可謂無功矣。而視再造乾坤、肇修人紀、復中國帝王所自立之天下，如我有功萬世之聖祖，則固霄壤懸絕矣。比而同之，可乎？後来臨御，間有處罪之嚴，如《大誥》所載者，豈聖人治天下與其所以定天下者，道固不能不異歟？至《祖訓》一書，乃又不欲後世聖子神孫輒以嚴法繩下，且深戒後之臣下妄言以啓威虐者。然則救亂者之治天下，與繼統者之守天下，亦固無異道歟？我聖祖神謨偉烈，薄海内外，固已家傳人誦久矣。至於攘夷救亂、一念不嗜殺人之心，可比隆三代，以益綿運作於千萬年而不替者，則豈人人皆曉然
translation_en: …among their deeds, was there any that could approach even one ten-thousandth of what our Sagely Progenitor accomplished? None. The Han quelled the disorders of Qin and Wang Mang, the Tang those of Sui, and the Song those of the Five Dynasties. These four rulers certainly cannot be said to have lacked merit. Yet compared with our Sagely Progenitor, whose achievements benefit ten thousand generations—who remade Heaven and Earth, first restored the bonds of human society, and recovered the realm in which the emperors and kings of the Central Kingdom had established themselves—they were indeed as far apart as heaven and earth. Can they be compared and treated as equals? Later in his reign, there were occasional instances of severe punishment, such as those recorded in the Grand Pronouncements. Could it be that the Way by which a sage governs the realm must necessarily differ from that by which he pacifies it? Yet in the Ancestral Injunctions, he did not wish his sagely sons and divine grandsons of later generations readily to apply harsh laws to their subordinates; moreover, he sternly warned against later ministers recklessly making statements that would incite intimidation and cruelty. Does this mean, then, that the one who delivers the realm from disorder and governs it, and the successor who preserves it, indeed follow the same Way? Our Sagely Progenitor’s divine plans and mighty achievements have long been handed down in every household and recited by every person, throughout the lands within and beyond the seas. But as for his heart, intent on driving out the foreign peoples and ending disorder, and wholly free of delight in killing—a heart that could rival the glory of the Three Dynasties and further prolong the working of the dynastic destiny [?] for tens of millions of years without decline—can everyone clearly understand…

title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
無疑我請敬陳之以昭示天下
問宋史取周程張朱諸大儒言行述為列
傳而以道學名焉蓋前無此例而創為
之以崇正學也大儒在當時挺然以道
學自任而未嘗輒以道學自名流俗乃
從而名之又因而詆之後又以偽學目
之時君不察顧嚴為之禁焉何也說者
謂朱子集諸儒之大成今以其同時諸
儒言之有東嘉之學有永康之學有金
===
溪之學有金華廣漢之學其入德之門
不能無異也朱子果一一皆能集其大
成歟數子之學亦可得而聞其槩歟其
間有與朱子鼎立而為三者道學列傳
或載焉或不載焉其不載者豈以其學
猶有可議歟程子親授太極圖於周子
而朱子釋之義理精微殆無餘蘊金溪
於此乃不能無疑焉何歟易簡支離之
論終以不合而今之學者顧欲強而同

不能無異也朱子果一一皆能集其大
成歟數子之學亦可得而閒其繁歟其
間有與朱子鼎立而爲三者道學列傳
或載焉或不載焉其不載者豈以其學
猶有可議歟程子親授太極圖於周子
而朱子釋之義理精微殆無餘蘊金谿
於此乃不能無疑焉何歟易簡支離之
論終以不合而今之學者顧欲強而同
punctuated:
無疑？我請敬陳之，以昭示天下。

問：宋史取周、程、張、朱諸大儒言行，述為列傳，而以道學名焉。蓋前無此例，而創為之，以崇正學也。大儒在當時，挺然以道學自任，而未嘗輒以道學自名。流俗乃從而名之，又因而詆之，後又以偽學目之。時君不察，顧嚴為之禁焉，何也？說者謂朱子集諸儒之大成。今以其同時諸儒言之，有東嘉之學，有永康之學，有金溪之學，有金華、廣漢之學，其入德之門不能無異也。朱子果一一皆能集其大成歟？數子之學，亦可得而聞其槩歟？其間有與朱子鼎立而為三者，道學列傳或載焉，或不載焉。其不載者，豈以其學猶有可議歟？程子親授太極圖於周子，而朱子釋之，義理精微，殆無餘蘊。金溪於此乃不能無疑焉，何歟？易簡、支離之論，終以不合，而今之學者顧欲強而同
translation_en:
…without doubt? I beg leave to set this forth respectfully, to make it clearly known throughout the realm.

Question: The History of the Song took the words and deeds of the great Confucian scholars Zhou, Cheng, Zhang, and Zhu and compiled them into biographies under the heading “Learning of the Way.” There had been no precedent for this; the category was newly established to honor orthodox learning. In their own time, these great scholars steadfastly took responsibility for the Learning of the Way, yet never lightly claimed that designation for themselves. The vulgar, however, applied it to them and then used it to disparage them, later branding their teaching “spurious learning.” The rulers of the time failed to discern the truth and instead imposed strict prohibitions upon it. Why was this?

Commentators say that Master Zhu brought the teachings of the various Confucian scholars to their fullest synthesis. Yet among his contemporaries there were the schools of Dongjia, Yongkang, Jinxi, Jinhua, and Guanghan, whose approaches to entering into virtue inevitably differed. Did Master Zhu truly bring each and every one of their teachings to its fullest synthesis? Might we also hear an outline of the teachings of these several masters? Among them were those who stood alongside Master Zhu as three rival authorities. Some are included in the biographies of scholars of the Learning of the Way, while others are not. Were those omitted excluded because their teachings still contained points open to criticism?

Master Cheng personally transmitted the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate to Master Zhou [?], and Master Zhu expounded it, leaving scarcely any of its subtle moral principles unexplored. Yet Jinxi could not refrain from doubting it. Why was this? The debate over simplicity and ease versus fragmentation ultimately remained unresolved, yet scholars today would insist on forcing the two into agreement…

問：孔子有言：「政寬則民慢，慢則糾之以猛；猛則民殘，殘則濟之以寬。」此誠不易之論。後之言治者多矣。於周，吾得一人焉，曰子產。其言曰：「太上以德，其次莫如猛。」今考其相鄭之跡，豈皆猛政乎？於漢，吾得一人焉，曰孔明。其言曰：「治世以大德，不以小惠。」今考其治蜀之效，豈皆大德乎？他如好古教化之在潁川，而或失之僭踰；威制豪強之在京兆，而或過於鉤距；以儒飾吏之美，或貽輕儇之譏；以一
translation_en:
…what, indeed, is the insight behind bringing them into agreement? Could it be that they delight in the apparent ease of that approach and wish covertly to disparage the learning of our Master Zhu? If we examine their intentions, are they really so very different from the likes of He Dan and Chen Jia? Some even commit their views to writing and openly indulge in disparagement to gain acceptance for their private opinions. Would there be anything objectionable in the ritual officials invoking precedents from the reigns of our imperial ancestors, burning their books, and prohibiting and repudiating their teachings? To honor orthodox learning without being misled by divergent doctrines, and thereby seek to fulfill His Majesty’s lofty intention of unifying moral principles so as to bring uniformity to customs—this is what we expect of you students. Please speak fully and conceal nothing.
Question: Confucius said: “When government is lenient, the people grow lax; when they grow lax, correct them with severity. When government is severe, the people suffer injury; when they suffer injury, relieve them with leniency.” This is indeed an unalterable judgment. Many have subsequently discussed government. In the Zhou period, I find one such man: Zichan. He said: “The highest form of government employs virtue; next to that, nothing equals severity.” Yet if we now examine his record as chief minister of Zheng, did it consist entirely of severe government? In the Han period, I find one such man: Kongming. He said: “Govern the world through great virtue, not through petty favors.” Yet if we now examine the results of his government of Shu, were they all manifestations of great virtue? There are other examples: devotion to antiquity and moral instruction in Yingchuan, which nevertheless sometimes erred through overstepping proper bounds; the use of stern authority to restrain powerful local magnates in Jingzhao, which nevertheless sometimes went too far in probing and trapping people; the admirable practice of adorning administrative service with Confucian learning, which nevertheless sometimes invited criticism for frivolous cleverness; using one…

text:
警百敏矣未免簿書之累其於禮樂刑
政之本似槩乎其未有得者而又焉知
剛柔時措之道哉今天下田晦之愁歎
未絕不可謂不殘閭閻之遊食相繼不
可謂不慢茲欲振民脩政由二子之所
以為治者擴而大之以求合乎聖人所
言之理當必有術願明言之將以告夫
治民者
問泰之九二朋亡與包荒並稱洪範五皇
===
極亦以朋淫為戒聖人之為世慮深矣
甘陵分部牛李爭權漢唐覆轍可為永
鑒夫何宋人不戒甘心蹈之其榜朝堂
諭百官士罹斥逐旋復收用猶有可諉
者自夫議論主於紹述政事繫於紀元
卒之正不勝邪國事以去不謂之人謀
不臧不可也其所以致此者何人而所
以主此者何說有可得而言者歟當時
豈無錄人之過不宜太深之說乎亦豈

punctuated:
警百，敏矣，未免簿書之累。其於禮樂刑政之本，似槩乎其未有得者，而又焉知剛柔時措之道哉？今天下田晦之愁歎未絕，不可謂不殘；閭閻之遊食相繼，不可謂不慢。茲欲振民脩政，由二子之所以為治者擴而大之，以求合乎聖人所言之理，當必有術。願明言之，將以告夫治民者。
問：泰之九二，朋亡與包荒並稱；《洪範》五皇極，亦以朋淫為戒。聖人之為世慮深矣！甘陵分部，牛李爭權，漢唐覆轍，可為永鑒。夫何宋人不戒，甘心蹈之？其榜朝堂、諭百官，士罹斥逐，旋復收用，猶有可諉者。自夫議論主於紹述，政事繫於紀元，卒之正不勝邪，國事以去，不謂之人謀不臧，不可也。其所以致此者何人，而所以主此者何說，有可得而言者歟？當時豈無錄人之過不宜太深之說乎？亦豈
translation_en:
…to warn a hundred was efficient indeed, yet it did not escape the burdens of clerical paperwork. As for the foundations of rites, music, punishments, and government, these men seem generally to have failed to grasp them. How, then, could they have understood the way of applying firmness and gentleness as circumstances require? Today, throughout the realm, sorrowful lamentations over the gloom in the fields [?] have not ceased: one cannot say that harshness is absent. In the villages, those who live idly at others’ expense appear one after another: one cannot say that laxity is absent. If we now wish to bring relief to the people and put government in order, extending and enlarging the methods by which those two men governed so as to accord with the principles stated by the sage, there must surely be a means. Please explain it clearly, so that it may be conveyed to those who govern the people.
Question: In the second nine of the hexagram Tai, “abandoning partisan attachments” is mentioned together with “embracing the uncultivated.” The fifth division of the Great Plan, “The August Ultimate,” likewise warns against excessive partisanship. Profound indeed was the sage’s concern for the world! The division into factions at Ganling and the struggle for power between Niu and Li—the disastrous precedents of the Han and Tang—can serve as lasting warnings. Why did the men of the Song fail to heed them and willingly follow the same course? As for posting proclamations at the court and issuing admonitions to the officials, while scholars suffered dismissal and expulsion only to be reinstated soon afterward, there might still be some excuse. But once political debate came to center on carrying forward the predecessors’ policies, and government affairs became bound to changes of reign era, the upright ultimately failed to overcome the wicked, and the affairs of state fell into ruin. This cannot but be called a failure of human counsel. Who brought this about, and what doctrines sustained it? Can these matters be explained? Was there not at the time a saying that one should not probe too deeply when recording others’ faults? And was there not also…

title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
無言語文字不可罪人之說乎謀國雖
遠言苦不行何歟使能恢九二包荒之
量推皇極大受之公則小人自無以投
君子之隙君子自有以制小人之變又
何黨之足憂哉何諸賢處此不能然也
世儒有著論以辨真偽者矣又因賛五
代六臣而反復致意以示戒矣又有續
其師之所論者矣彼其同道同心之語
固謂君子有朋而嘉禾惡草之喻又謂
===
君子無黨至謂蔽耳目去善類言尤痛
切則其所係又不止於一時治忽其言
果孰然而孰否邪國家無事之時士大
夫未可遽為朋黨之說一時言之雖若
無甚利害萬一他日或為奸人之資則
雖極力救之亦已無及於事矣方今
聖明在上大小羣臣莫不精白一心以承
休德善則相師過則相規固無朋黨之足慮
特以前代君臣得失與凡前賢議論同

無言語文字不可罪人之說乎？謀國雖遠，言苦不行，何歟？使能恢九二包荒之量，推皇極大受之公，則小人自無以投君子之隙，君子自有以制小人之變，又何黨之足憂哉？何諸賢處此不能然也？世儒有著論以辨真偽者矣，又因賛五代六臣而反復致意以示戒矣，又有續其師之所論者矣。彼其同道同心之語，固謂君子有朋；而嘉禾惡草之喻，又謂君子無黨。至謂蔽耳目、去善類，言尤痛切，則其所係又不止於一時治忽。其言果孰然而孰否邪？國家無事之時，士大夫未可遽為朋黨之說。一時言之，雖若無甚利害，萬一他日或為奸人之資，則雖極力救之，亦已無及於事矣。
方今聖明在上，大小羣臣莫不精白一心以承休德，善則相師，過則相規，固無朋黨之足慮。特以前代君臣得失與凡前賢議論同
translation_en:
…was there not also the argument that people should not be condemned for their spoken or written words? Though such counsel for the state was far-sighted, it suffered from never being put into practice. Why was this? Had they been able to enlarge their capacity to “embrace the uncultivated,” as in the second yang line of the Book of Changes, and extend the impartiality of the “great acceptance” taught in the August Norm, petty men would naturally have had no opening through which to exploit divisions among gentlemen, and gentlemen would naturally have had the means to counter the intrigues of petty men. What factions, then, would there have been to fear? Why were those worthy men unable to act thus in these circumstances?
Scholars have written discourses distinguishing the true from the false. Others have repeatedly pressed their warnings in an appraisal of the six ministers of the Five Dynasties; still others have continued their teachers’ arguments. The statement about sharing the same Way and the same purpose indeed holds that gentlemen have fellowships, whereas the analogy of fine grain and noxious weeds holds that gentlemen have no factions. As for the claim that factions obstruct the ruler’s eyes and ears and drive away good men, its language is especially anguished and forceful: the stakes extend beyond order or disorder at any one time. Which of these statements, then, is right, and which is wrong? When the state is free from trouble, scholar-officials should not hastily advance arguments about factions. Though such talk may seem to have little consequence at the time, should it one day furnish wicked men with a means to act, even the utmost efforts to remedy the situation would come too late.
Now our sagely and enlightened sovereign reigns above, and all his ministers, great and small, purify their intentions and unite their hearts in upholding his splendid virtue. They learn from one another’s good deeds and admonish one another for their faults. There is assuredly no cause to fear factions. Yet the successes and failures of rulers and ministers of earlier dynasties, together with the agreements among the arguments of former worthies…

title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
異有足為世鑒者不可以不講也故願
與爾諸士子論之
問井田先王治天下之大經大法也自孟
子之世蓋已不得聞其詳矣請以今日
之事言之分封茅土不加於有周之多
也而
藩府之需每稱不足繼今支派益衍將何以
給之東南漕運不減於
國初之舊也而太倉之蓄不聞露積脫有水
===
旱蠲免將何以充之邊儲出於田也諸
鎮飛輓不可謂不勤矣一有征調至出
内帑沿邊屯種得無有侵漁之患乎馬政出
於田也民間孳牧不可謂不勞矣一有
耗折輒給官價各郡苑地得無有兼并
之弊乎他如徭役均矣而民未甚蘇驛
傳清矣而下數告困水利非不修也而
堙塞之害固在農桑非不勸也而蠶織
之政漸衰凡此皆吾

translation_en:
…differences of opinion that can serve as lessons for the world must be examined. Thus I wish to discuss them with you candidates.
Question: The well-field system was a fundamental principle and great institution by which the ancient kings governed the realm. Yet even in Mencius’s time, its details could apparently no longer be learned. Let us discuss this in terms of present circumstances. The granting of fiefs, ceremonially conferred with earth wrapped in thatch, is no more extensive than under the Zhou, yet the princely establishments continually report that their needs are inadequately supplied. As their collateral branches multiply hereafter, how will they be provided for? Grain shipments from the southeast are no smaller than they were at the founding of the dynasty, yet we do not hear that the reserves of the capital’s Taicang granary overflow into outdoor stockpiles. Should floods or droughts necessitate tax remissions, how will those reserves be replenished? Frontier provisions come from the fields. The garrisons cannot be said to lack diligence in transporting supplies with all speed; yet whenever troops are mobilized, even the imperial treasury must be drawn upon. Might the agricultural colonies along the frontier be suffering from encroachment and extortion? Horse administration, too, depends upon the fields. The common people cannot be said to spare their toil in breeding and pasturing horses; yet whenever losses occur, official funds must be disbursed to purchase replacements. Might the pasturelands of the various prefectures be subject to wrongful engrossment? In other matters, labor-service obligations have been equalized, yet the people have obtained little relief; abuses in the postal relay service have been cleared away, yet those below repeatedly report distress. Irrigation works have certainly been repaired, yet the harm caused by silting and blockage persists. text:
國與吾民必於田焉資之者也當何術以處
之歟夫無君子莫治野人無野人莫養
君子士亦食其養矣願聞其所以治之
之道

translation_en: …the state and our people must depend upon the fields for all these things. By what methods should these matters be addressed? Without gentlemen, there would be no one to govern the people of the countryside; without the people of the countryside, there would be no one to support gentlemen. You scholars, too, receive your sustenance from them. I wish to hear the principles by which you would govern them.

First Session

Four Books

“When the gentleman studies broadly in cultural learning and restrains himself through ritual propriety, surely he may avoid straying from the Way!”

Zheng Xiao

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Supervising Secretary: “This composition is refined and restrained, with a lingering depth of meaning. In sum, your learning [?] is indeed broad, yet capable of being held within bounds.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Ye, Compiler: “Breadth of learning and restraint, pursued in their proper order without partiality to either, were the means by which Master Yan aspired to sagehood. This composition grasps this. Has its author perhaps devoted careful thought to the learning through which one aspires to emulate Yan?”

Comment by Associate Examiner Huang, Compiler: “Writers in the examination hall generally strive for elaborate composition, yet stray from the true meaning. This composition proceeds in a plain and even manner, its meaning fully sufficient in itself. It may likewise be said not to stray from principle.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Lü, Senior Compiler: “It clearly explains how breadth of learning and restraint complement one another. If scholars can put this into practice, they too may approach the Way.”

Comment by Examiner Shi, Academician: “The wording is not prolix, yet the meaning is fully conveyed.”

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Grand Secretary: “The wording conveys the principle; it merits inclusion.”

title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
道也學而得其方焉其於道也夫何背畔之有
夫子教人為學之法如此今夫道之在天下者
散於萬殊而會於一本惟其散於萬殊也求以
知之不可以不學而學有不博則所知未至也
君子必於文而博之凡先王之法布在方冊者
舉其大不遺其細以廣乎吾之所聞凡率性之
理具諸事物者會其粗必及其精以大乎吾之
所見而不使其聰明之德有未盡焉惟其會於
一本也有所得焉不可以不守而守有弗要則
===
所得未固也君子必約之以禮焉即其所真知
而反之實踐加乎其身者必矩度之不踰取其
所心得而見之躬行發於其事者視品節以為
準而不使於中正之則有或謬焉君子之學如
是何以不背於道邪盖文者道之粲然者也不
先之以博則知必有蔽而不免於固陋禮者道
之歸宿者也不反之以約則行有未至而不免
於支離今博以開其約之端而知與行並進則
有所持循不惑於似是之非道由是可入也雖

punctuated: 道也。學而得其方焉，其於道也，夫何背畔之有？夫子教人為學之法如此。今夫道之在天下者，散於萬殊而會於一本。惟其散於萬殊也，求以知之，不可以不學；而學有不博，則所知未至也。君子必於文而博之：凡先王之法布在方冊者，舉其大，不遺其細，以廣乎吾之所聞；凡率性之理具諸事物者，會其粗，必及其精，以大乎吾之所見，而不使其聰明之德有未盡焉。惟其會於一本也，有所得焉，不可以不守；而守有弗要，則所得未固也。君子必約之以禮焉：即其所真知而反之實踐，加乎其身者，必矩度之不踰；取其所心得而見之躬行，發於其事者，視品節以為準，而不使於中正之則有或謬焉。君子之學如是，何以不背於道邪？盖文者，道之粲然者也。不先之以博，則知必有蔽，而不免於固陋。禮者，道之歸宿者也。不反之以約，則行有未至，而不免於支離。今博以開其約之端，而知與行並進，則有所持循，不惑於似是之非，道由是可入也。雖
translation_en:
…the Way. If, in learning, one finds the proper method, how could one turn away from the Way? Such is the method of learning that the Master teaches.

Now, the Way as it exists throughout the world is dispersed among myriad particulars yet converges upon a single root. Precisely because it is dispersed among myriad particulars, one cannot seek to understand it without learning; and if that learning lacks breadth, one’s understanding will remain incomplete. The gentleman must therefore broaden his learning through cultural writings. As for the laws of the former kings set down in books, he takes up their major principles without omitting their finer details, thereby enlarging what he has heard. As for the principles of following one’s nature embodied in affairs and things, he comprehends their broad outlines and must also reach their subtleties, thereby enlarging what he has perceived. Thus he leaves none of his capacities for hearing and understanding unrealized.

Precisely because the Way converges upon a single root, whatever one has grasped must be preserved; and if one’s means of preserving it fails to grasp the essentials, what one has gained will not be secure. The gentleman must therefore discipline himself through ritual propriety. He takes what he truly knows and brings it back to actual practice, ensuring that whatever pertains to his own person does not overstep the prescribed measures. He takes what he has grasped in his heart and manifests it in personal conduct, using the gradations and restraints of ritual propriety as the standard for what issues in his affairs. Thus he allows no deviation from the norm of centrality and correctness.

With the gentleman’s learning proceeding in this way, why does he not turn away from the Way? Cultural writings are the radiant manifestation of the Way. Unless one begins with breadth of learning, one’s understanding will inevitably be obscured, and one cannot avoid narrow-mindedness. Ritual propriety is where the Way ultimately rests. Unless one returns to disciplined restraint, one’s conduct will remain deficient, and one cannot avoid fragmentation. Now, when breadth of learning opens the way to disciplined restraint, and knowledge and action advance together, one has something to uphold and follow and is not misled by errors that appear correct. Through this one can enter the Way. Although…

title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
未與之為一而亦豈至於判而二哉約以收其
博之功而行與知互發則有所依據不偏於無
用之體道自是不遠也雖未與之脗合而亦豈
至於背而馳哉吁知博約不可以偏廢則為學
有不易之方知博約僅可以弗畔則為學有不
已之功茲固聖門之至教而君子所由以入聖
者乎抑是言也顏子嘗述之矣觀其曰夫子循
循然善誘人則知聖門之教唯此二事而已然

未與之為一，而亦豈至於判而二哉？約以收其博之功，而行與知互發，則有所依據，不偏於無用之體，道自是不遠也。雖未與之脗合，而亦豈至於背而馳哉？吁！知博約不可以偏廢，則為學有不易之方；知博約僅可以弗畔，則為學有不已之功。茲固聖門之至教，而君子所由以入聖者乎？抑是言也，顏子嘗述之矣。觀其曰：「夫子循循然善誘人。」則知聖門之教唯此二事而已。然考諸精一之論，自虞廷固已發之。盖聖賢傳心之要法，不容少易焉者，故堯授舜，舜授禹，而未嘗有所變焉。夫子之後，其說益長，其為教益明矣。學者循是以求之，宜易為力，而有道之士卒不多見，無亦自棄於聖人也歟？

上律天時，下襲水土。
藍田

translation_en:
…not yet become one with the Way, how could he go so far as to become divided from it, as two separate things? By using restraint to gather in the fruits of broad learning, so that practice and knowledge bring each other forth, he has something to rely upon and does not incline toward substance devoid of practical use. The Way is consequently not far off. Although he has not yet become fully united with it, how could he turn his back on it and hasten away? Ah! To know that neither breadth nor restraint may be neglected is to possess an unchanging method of learning; to know that breadth and restraint can do no more than keep one from departing from the Way is to recognize that the work of learning never ends. Is this not indeed the highest teaching of the sage’s school, and the means by which the gentleman enters sagehood? Moreover, Master Yan once recounted these very words. When we consider his statement, “The Master skillfully guides people forward step by step,” we know that the teaching of the sage’s school consists solely of these two matters. Yet if we examine the discussion of refinement and singleness of mind, it had already been articulated at the court of Shun. These are the essential methods by which sages and worthies transmit the mind, admitting not the slightest alteration. Thus Yao handed them down to Shun, and Shun to Yu, without ever changing them. After the Master, their exposition became ever fuller, and their teaching ever clearer. If learners follow this path in their pursuit, they should readily be able to make progress. Yet men who possess the Way are, in the end, seldom seen. Could it be that they themselves abandon the prospect of attaining sagehood?

“Above, he took the seasons of Heaven as his rule; below, he followed the conditions of water and soil.”
By Lan Tian.

Only in this piece have I found language that is concise yet fully conveys the principles. I have selected it for inclusion.

Associate Examiner Zhang, Left Supervising Secretary, comments: “The wording is concise and profound. An exposition of the meaning of the Doctrine of the Mean should be like this.”
Associate Examiner Lin, Examining Editor, comments: “The passages on taking Heaven above as a standard and following the earth below show a true and penetrating understanding. This, too, is someone who speaks well of the sage.”
Associate Examiner Ma, Compiler, comments: “The Way of Heaven and the virtue of the sage are exceedingly difficult to describe. This composition may well be said to describe them skillfully.”
Examiner Shi, Academician, comments: “This is writing that elucidates principle.”
Examiner Jiang, Grand Secretary, comments: “Superior to the other compositions.”
The sage looks upward to take the Way of Heaven as his model and downward to follow the Way of Earth. Vast indeed are the Ways of Heaven and Earth! Who but the consummate sage of the world could take them as his model and follow them? Chapter Thirty of the Doctrine of the Mean elucidates the Way of Heaven through the sageliness of Kongzi. Its meaning is that what makes Kongzi a sage surely goes beyond honoring the Way of Yao and Shun and observing the models of Kings Wen and Wu. That which establishes the Way of Heaven is called yin and yang; these spread forth to constitute the four seasons. Though said to be difficult to fathom, when one looks upward to observe their workings, there is a spontaneous natural order above. The sage takes this as his standard. Thus the myriad distinctions are united in one root: he follows the Way according to the time, without deviation. Perfect harmony issues from supreme centrality: he moves together with the times, without impediment. His taking office or withdrawing, his speaking or remaining silent, accord wholly with the pattern of waning and waxing, fullness and emptiness. His rising and retiring, eating and resting, accord wholly with the workings of movement and stillness, closing and opening. text:
地之道曰柔與剛比而為水土雖曰異齊也而
俯察其理則有一定者在下焉襲之是盖居方
辨物因其俗而不違安土敦仁素其位而無失
隨寓而安一流行坎止之常也居易以俟一含
弘貞靜之體也所謂無入而不自得者是已非
因乎地道而何是則陰陽成象也而聖人之道
其即陰陽不測之神剛柔成質也而聖人之道
其即剛柔相推之化參三才而兩之其斯以為

地之道曰柔與剛，比而為水土，雖曰異齊也，而俯察其理，則有一定者在下焉，襲之。是盖居方辨物，因其俗而不違；安土敦仁，素其位而無失。隨寓而安，一流行坎止之常也；居易以俟，一含弘貞靜之體也。所謂「無入而不自得」者，是已。非因乎地道而何？是則陰陽成象也，而聖人之道，其即陰陽不測之神；剛柔成質也，而聖人之道，其即剛柔相推之化。參三才而兩之，其斯以為孔子也歟！《中庸》發明天人之理，無餘蘊矣。抑《中庸》一書，子思憂道學之失其傳而作也，故於天道人道反復言之，而每實以堯舜文武周公孔子之事。盖欲學者即其所見聞者而取則焉，則由賢而聖，由聖而天矣。噫！天不可幾而及也，聖人不可易而至也。由明而誠，其庶幾矣乎！

堯舜之道，不以仁政，不能平治天下。
陳儒

translation_en:
…the Way of Earth is called yielding and firm. These combine to form water and soil. Though their dispositions differ [?], when one looks down and examines their principles, there is a fixed order below, which he follows. Thus he occupies his place and distinguishes things, accommodating local customs without violating them; he rests content in his land and deepens his benevolence, acting according to his station without error. To be at ease wherever he finds himself embodies the constant rule of flowing onward when the way is open and stopping when a pit is encountered. To dwell in ease and await what comes embodies capaciousness, breadth, steadfastness, and stillness. This is what is meant by “There is no situation in which he is not at ease with himself.” What could this be but following the Way of Earth? Thus yin and yang produce configurations, and the sage’s Way is precisely the unfathomable spiritual efficacy of yin and yang; the firm and yielding produce material forms, and the sage’s Way is precisely the transformation wrought by their mutual interaction. Bringing together the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity—and doubling them: is this not what makes Confucius who he is? The Doctrine of the Mean elucidates the principles of Heaven and humanity, leaving nothing unexplored.

Moreover, Zisi wrote the Doctrine of the Mean because he feared that the learning of the Way would lose its transmission. Thus he speaks repeatedly of the Way of Heaven and the Way of humanity, always substantiating his account with the deeds of Yao, Shun, Wen, Wu, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius. His intention was that students should draw models from what they had seen and heard. They could then advance from worthiness to sagehood, and from sagehood to Heaven. Alas! Heaven cannot be reached merely by aspiring to it, nor can sagehood be attained easily. Yet by proceeding from understanding to sincerity, might one come close?

“Even with the Way of Yao and Shun, without benevolent government one cannot bring peace and order to All under Heaven.”
By Chen Ru.

Comment by Associate Examiner Xue, a Bureau Secretary: “The writing is concise and apt. It can serve as a model for those who prize florid extravagance.”

Even those in antiquity who fully realized the way of the ruler could not achieve good government apart from standards. Standards are the instruments of government. text:
幾焉莫不本精神心術以達於綱維其見於天
下也有庶政焉莫不推至誠惻怛以形諸規制
是以黎民於變煥乎文章之著見也四方風動
秩乎府事之修和也使其有是心焉而綱維有
所未備吾恐德隱於中而澤不下究一身之外
且不能及矣九州之大其何以理之乎堯舜雖
曰至聖將有不得用其聖者矣有是仁焉而規
制有所未周吾恐勢限於外而德不廣被一家
之近且不能保矣四海之遠其何以馭之乎堯
===

以為治在聖人有所不可而況非聖人者哉君
天下者宜知所務矣抑嘗聞世儒有言古之治
天下者純任道後之治天下者純任法揆諸孟

以為治在聖人有所不可而況非聖人者哉君
天下者宜知所務矣抑嘗聞世儒有言古之治
天下者純任道後之治天下者純任法揆諸孟
氏所論若有不同焉者何哉蓋帝王之所謂政
兼道與法而言之若堯舜之仁政是已後世之
所謂法則外道而徒事於智力之私僅足以為
把持天下之具未可與帝王之治同日而語也
有志於帝王之治者其尚以堯舜為準哉
punctuated:
幾焉，莫不本精神心術以達於綱維；其見於天下也，有庶政焉，莫不推至誠惻怛以形諸規制。是以黎民於變，煥乎文章之著見也；四方風動，秩乎府事之修和也。使其有是心焉，而綱維有所未備，吾恐德隱於中，而澤不下究，一身之外且不能及矣，九州之大，其何以理之乎？堯舜雖曰至聖，將有不得用其聖者矣。有是仁焉，而規制有所未周，吾恐勢限於外，而德不廣被，一家之近且不能保矣，四海之遠，其何以馭之乎？堯舜雖曰至治，將有不得施其治者矣。夫舍法度以為治，在聖人有所不可，而況非聖人者哉！君天下者宜知所務矣。
抑嘗聞世儒有言：「古之治天下者純任道，後之治天下者純任法。」揆諸孟氏所論，若有不同焉者，何哉？蓋帝王之所謂政，兼道與法而言之，若堯舜之仁政是已。後世之所謂法，則外道而徒事於智力之私，僅足以為把持天下之具，未可與帝王之治同日而語也。有志於帝王之治者，其尚以堯舜為準哉！
translation_en:
…the myriad affairs of state: all draw upon the spirit and the dispositions of the mind and find expression in the governing framework. As manifested throughout the realm, there are the various affairs of government: all extend utmost sincerity and compassion into institutional arrangements. Thus the common people are transformed, splendidly displaying civilized refinement; the four quarters respond as grass bends before the wind, and the business of government is conducted in orderly harmony. Suppose they possessed such a heart, yet their governing framework remained incomplete. I fear that their virtue would remain concealed within and their beneficence would fail to reach those below. It could not extend even beyond their own persons; how, then, could they bring order to the vast Nine Provinces? Though Yao and Shun were called the greatest sages, they would have no means to put their sagacity to use. Suppose they possessed such benevolence, yet their institutional arrangements were not comprehensive. I fear that outward circumstances would constrain them and their virtue would not spread widely. They could not safeguard even their own households, so close at hand; how, then, could they govern the distant reaches within the Four Seas? Though Yao and Shun were credited with perfect governance, they would have no means to carry it out. Even sages cannot govern by abandoning laws and standards; how much less can those who are not sages! Those who rule the realm should know where to direct their efforts.
Yet I have heard scholars of our age say: “Those who governed the realm in antiquity relied wholly on the Way; those who governed it in later ages relied wholly on law.” Judged against Mencius’s discussion, this seems to differ. Why is that? What the ancient emperors and kings called government encompassed both the Way and law, as exemplified by the benevolent government of Yao and Shun. What later ages called law, however, excluded the Way and merely pursued selfish ends through cleverness and force. It sufficed only as an instrument for maintaining a grip on the realm and cannot be spoken of in the same breath as the government of the ancient emperors and kings. Let those who aspire to such government take Yao and Shun as their standard!

translation_en:
Book of Changes

Guan (Contemplation): “The ritual washing has been performed, but the offering has not yet been presented. There is sincerity and an appearance of solemn dignity; those below behold it and are transformed.”

Lu Quan

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Acting Bureau Director: “In explaining what it means to serve as an exemplar for contemplation, his wording is most carefully weighed. This is quite different from indulging in superficial rhetoric.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Left Supervising Secretary: “The language and tone are substantial and dignified—truly writing befitting a flourishing age. Include it.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Hanlin Reviewing Editor: “He proceeds with a straightforward, even exposition, and the meaning of the hexagram statement emerges naturally from his explanation. An excellent composition. Include it: it can serve as a model.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Ma, Hanlin Compiler: “Concise, clear, pure, and refined: a superlative exposition of the meaning of the Changes.”

Comment by Examiner Shi, Academician: “This is precisely the meaning of the Commentary on the Judgments.”

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Grand Secretary: “As for the meaning of the judgment on Guan, among the rambling compositions in the examination hall, I have seen only this essay [?].”

The sage fully possesses the virtue required to serve as an exemplar for contemplation, and thereby brings about transformation through nonaction. How profound is the marvelous power of perfect virtue to move others and reach their hearts! When the sage above possesses virtue in its fullness and those below behold him, how could any remain untransformed? The meaning of the Commentary on the Judgments is that the hexagram Guan signifies displaying oneself for others to behold. King Wen appended the words, “The ritual washing has been performed, but the offering has not yet been presented. There is sincerity and an appearance of solemn dignity.” This indeed is the great…

title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
觀聖人以巽順中正之德在修道立教之位藏
乎身者淵微莫測其居上而示下也惟在於一
誠用於民者機緘不露其居尊而臨卑也不外
乎恭敬清明在躬儼乎四方之則也齊莊有敬
巍乎萬夫之望也有如祭者當方盥未薦之時
極其孚誠而顯然可仰者焉由是誠能動物凡
得於仰止者莫不遷善以自新信以發志凡得
於利見者莫不鼓舞以相慶枉者化於直詖者
化於平蓋自百官以至於萬民熙熙乎不知帝
力之何有於我也近者移其習遠者移其風蓋
自邦畿以至於荒服蕩蕩乎不知帝德之何以
能名也夫德備於一身而化成於天下聖人為
觀之道豈復加於此哉彖傳之旨精矣抑又論
之德以化民固也然必有政焉而後天下可從
而理也否則徒善而已故彖傳曰觀民設教九
五曰觀我生爻所以深明夫不輕自用之理蓋
非終不用也特不輕於用焉耳後世不知此義
而以清淨為無為其去堯舜也遠矣言治道者

化於乎蓋自百官以至於萬民熙熙乎不知帝
===
力之何有於我也近者移其習遠者移其風蓋
自邦畿以至於荒服蕩蕩乎不知帝德之何以
能名也夫德備於一身而化成於天下聖人爲
觀之道豈復加於此哉彖傳之旨精矣抑又論
之德以化民固也然必有政焉而後天下可從
而理也否則徒善而已故彖傳曰觀民設教九
五曰觀我生又所以深明夫不離自用之理蓋
非終不用也特不輕於用焉耳後世不知此義
而以清淨爲無爲其去堯舜也遠矣言治道者
punctuated:
觀聖人以巽順中正之德，在修道立教之位，藏乎身者淵微莫測，其居上而示下也，惟在於一誠；用於民者機緘不露，其居尊而臨卑也，不外乎恭敬。清明在躬，儼乎四方之則也；齊莊有敬，巍乎萬夫之望也。有如祭者當方盥未薦之時，極其孚誠，而顯然可仰者焉。由是，誠能動物，凡得於仰止者，莫不遷善以自新；信以發志，凡得於利見者，莫不鼓舞以相慶。枉者化於直，詖者化於平，蓋自百官以至於萬民，熙熙乎不知帝力之何有於我也。近者移其習，遠者移其風，蓋自邦畿以至於荒服，蕩蕩乎不知帝德之何以能名也。夫德備於一身，而化成於天下，聖人為觀之道，豈復加於此哉？彖傳之旨精矣！

抑又論之，德以化民，固也；然必有政焉，而後天下可從而理也。否則徒善而已。故彖傳曰：「觀民設教。」九五曰：「觀我生。」爻所以深明夫不輕自用之理，蓋非終不用也，特不輕於用焉耳。後世不知此義，而以清淨為無為，其去堯舜也遠矣！言治道者
translation_en:
…the sage who serves as the great exemplar possesses the virtues of humility, compliance, centrality, and correctness, and occupies the position from which he cultivates the Way and establishes instruction. What he holds within himself is profound, subtle, and unfathomable; in dwelling above and showing an example to those below, he relies solely upon sincerity. In his dealings with the people, the workings remain concealed; in occupying an exalted position and presiding over the lowly, he never goes beyond reverence and respect. Clarity and discernment reside in his person: augustly he stands as the standard for the four quarters. Solemn, dignified, and reverent, he stands loftily as the object of all people’s hopes. He resembles one conducting a sacrifice at the moment when he has washed his hands but has not yet presented the offerings: his trustworthiness and sincerity reach their utmost, and he is manifestly worthy of reverence. Thus sincerity moves other beings, and all who benefit from looking up to him turn toward goodness and renew themselves. Trustworthiness awakens their aspirations, and all who benefit from seeing him are inspired to rejoice together. The crooked are transformed into the upright, and the biased into the impartial. From the hundred officials down to the myriad people, all live in harmony and happiness, unaware of what the emperor’s power has done for them. Those nearby change their habits, and those far away change their customs. From the royal domain to the remotest regions, his virtue is so vast that none knows how to name it. When virtue is complete in a single person and moral transformation is accomplished throughout the world, what more could there be to the sage’s way of serving as an exemplar? How profound is the meaning of the Commentary on the Judgments!

Yet let us consider this further. That virtue transforms the people is certainly true; nevertheless, there must also be government before the world can be brought to order. Otherwise, there is merely goodness on its own. Thus the Commentary on the Judgments says, “Observe the people and establish instruction,” and the nine in the fifth place says, “Observe my life.” This line elucidates the principle of not rashly putting one’s own capacities to use. It does not mean never using them, but simply not using them lightly. Later generations failed to understand this meaning and took purity and quietude to constitute nonaction. How far removed they were from Yao and Shun! Those who discuss the way of governing…

translation_en:
… One should consider them together.

“Through ease and simplicity, the principles of all under Heaven are grasped. When those principles are grasped, one establishes one’s position in their midst.”
By Wang Dian 汪滇.

Associate Examiner Liu, Acting Bureau Director, comments: “The wording defining ease and simplicity is most apt, and the transitions are especially refined. Moreover, bringing out the two terms ‘virtue’ and ‘achievement’ at the essay’s close makes the exposition still clearer and more complete. Has he not grasped the principles of all under Heaven?”

Associate Examiner Zhang, Left Supervising Secretary, comments: “The learning of human nature and principle is expressed in just a few phrases, without a single word allowing any lapse. Surely this is an accomplished writer.”

Associate Examiner Lin, Examining Editor, comments: “The language is concise, and the explanation of principle precise. This is how the meaning of the Changes should be expounded.”

Associate Examiner Ma, Compiler, comments: “He brings out the depths of purity, tranquility, subtlety, and refinement, without difficult, abstruse, strained, or obscure language. Has he, too, attained an understanding of ease and simplicity?”

Examiner Shi, Academician, comments: “The explanation of how ease and simplicity, at their utmost, can encompass the principles of all under Heaven is clear and exhaustive.”

Examiner Jiang, Grand Secretary, comments: “How could anyone without a profound understanding of the Changes attain this?”

Only by embodying the Way and reaching its utmost can one establish the ultimate standard for humanity. For Qian is ease and Kun is simplicity …

title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
而天下之理不外是也體道而造其極則理無
不得矣其成人位而參天地也宜哉大傳論乾
坤之理分見於造化而人兼體之至此蓋謂乾
坤之道易簡而已體乾之易至賢人之德而弗
已焉則乾之易即吾之易精義之妙殆與知始
者同一機矣法坤之簡至賢人之業而益進焉
則坤之簡即吾之簡時措之宜殆與作成者無
二致矣吾見知能合德而成性以存外內合一
而大本以立天下之理雖曰散於萬殊也其根
===
柢在是矣固可以該括之而無遺天下之事雖
曰各具一理也其樞紐在是矣亦可以貫通之
而無失夫易簡而天下之理得如此何以成位
乎其中哉蓋天以易而位乎上也吾之易有以
上配乎天地以簡而位乎下也吾之簡有以下
配乎地德則日新之德而天地之化育將賴之
以範圍參為三才一屹然中處之位也夫何愧
哉業則富有之業而萬物之性命將藉之以曲
成配乎兩儀一卓然並立之體也又何慊哉夫

translation_en:
…and the principles of all under Heaven lie within these. If one embodies the Way and reaches its utmost, no principle remains uncomprehended. How fitting that one should thereby fulfill the human position and stand alongside Heaven and Earth! The Great Commentary discusses the principles of Qian and Kun, manifested separately in the workings of creation but embodied together in human beings. At this point, it means that the ways of Qian and Kun are simply ease and simplicity. By embodying Qian’s ease, attaining the virtue of a worthy person, and not stopping there, Qian’s ease becomes my own ease. The subtle mastery of refining one’s understanding of principles then operates through virtually the same impulse as that which governs beginnings. By modeling oneself on Kun’s simplicity, attaining the accomplishments of a worthy person, and advancing still further, Kun’s simplicity becomes my own simplicity. The fittingness of putting things into practice at the proper time then differs in no respect from that which brings things to completion. I see knowing and capacity unite in virtue, so that one’s perfected nature is preserved; the outward and inward become one, so that the great foundation is established. Although the principles of all under Heaven are dispersed among myriad different things, their root lies here: one can therefore encompass them without omission. Although each affair under Heaven possesses its own principle, their pivot lies here: one can therefore comprehend them throughout without error.
When ease and simplicity thus enable one to grasp the principles of all under Heaven, how does one establish one’s position between Heaven and Earth? Heaven occupies its place above through ease, and my ease enables me to match Heaven above. Earth occupies its place below through simplicity, and my simplicity enables me to match Earth below. As for virtue, it is virtue renewed daily: the transforming and nourishing activity of Heaven and Earth will depend on it for encompassing regulation. Joining them as one of the Three Powers, one occupies a firmly established position in their midst. What cause is there for shame? As for accomplishment, it is accomplishment abundant in its possessions: the nature and destiny of the myriad things will depend on it for fulfillment in each particular case. Matching the Two Modes, Heaven and Earth, one stands distinctly alongside them as a full counterpart. What deficiency could one feel? Now…

translation_en:
…Nothing is more manifold than the principles of all under Heaven, yet ease and simplicity encompass them all; nothing is greater than the positions of Heaven and Earth, yet ease and simplicity establish them. At this point, the sage’s accomplishments are complete. Examining the statements about ease and simplicity in the Great Commentary, we find that they refer to more than one thing: the patterns and models provided by the lines and images; the generation and completion of things through the creative transformations of nature; and the vigor and receptivity of the human mind. This chapter, however, speaks of ease and simplicity as realized by sages and worthies. In nature’s creative transformations, they are the heavenly mandate; in the human mind, they are its nature; in the lines and images, they are their principles. Sages and worthies are those who have investigated these principles fully, fulfilled their nature, and thereby attained understanding. In substance, these are all one. If learners take the principles of the Book of Changes and seek them within their own minds, the ease and simplicity of Heaven and Earth will be found within the small compass of their hearts. Let those who wish to fulfill the human Way ponder and deliberate upon this!

…indeed shows insight.

Associate Examiner Lü, Senior Compiler, comments: “The Way of the sages is fully comprehended in the single principle of the Mean; the learning of the sages rests upon questioning. This composition seems able to express this.”

Examiner Shi, Academician, comments: “Its analysis of the words ‘ample’ and ‘small’ is exceptionally precise. This is someone skilled at explaining principle.”

Examiner Jiang, Grand Secretary, comments: “Clear and fluent, without blemish.”

In a ruler’s learning, delight in drawing upon others brings abundance, while exclusive reliance upon oneself brings insufficiency. How profoundly true it is that nothing in learning is more precious than delight in asking questions! Otherwise, one merely makes oneself small. It was fitting, then, that the great minister of Shang should draw upon an ancient saying to exhort his ruler! His meaning was that a ruler, in striving to cultivate virtue and establish the Mean, must first devote himself to learning. How could he fail to delight in questioning and instead rely upon himself alone?

If he truly recognizes that his own intelligence is limited, whenever he has a doubt he will diligently pursue searching questions. If he clearly perceives that the moral principles of the world are inexhaustible, all his questioning will spring from heartfelt delight. If he delights in questioning in this way, I know that his knowledge will grow rich through gathering widely, and his understanding of ritual propriety and righteousness will become refined through accumulated learning. Inwardly, he will expand in heavenly virtue: how could it fail to become exalted? Outwardly, he will encompass affairs and undertakings: how could his scope fail to become broad? Though his single mind may be called small, it will be no different from Heaven and Earth in their covering and sustaining of all things. Is this not ample?

If, however, he acts without knowing, his judgments of right and wrong will be mired in his own opinions: ‘Let no one contradict what I say.’ If he proceeds without consulting others, his judgments of what is acceptable will follow his private inclinations, and he will disregard what others say. If, indeed, he relies upon himself…

translation_en:
…self-willed in this way, I know that his hearing in all four directions will become obstructed on every side, and ordinary men below him will be unable to express themselves fully. Inwardly, he cannot govern his mind, and his virtue thus stands isolated; outwardly, he cannot govern affairs, and all his undertakings fall into neglect. Though he may claim the insight of an independent understanding, how does this differ from peering through a tube or measuring with a ladle? Is this not narrowness? Thus, in learning, nothing is harder than attaining breadth, while narrowness is its affliction. If one wishes earnestly to seek breadth and escape the confines of narrowness, can one fail to understand where to direct one's efforts?

Generally speaking, people are not born knowing; they must rely on learning. From the Son of Heaven down to the common people, none has achieved success without following a teacher. In his counsel to Tang, Zhonghui discussed the way to win the allegiance of the feudal lords, extended his argument to cultivating virtue and disciplining oneself, and placed ultimate emphasis on being able to find a teacher for oneself. He also singled out the phrase “delighting in asking questions” to indicate the aim of sagely learning. Its purport is identical to Confucius's praise of Shun's delight in asking questions. Might this saying, then, already have existed in the time of Yao and Shun and been transmitted down to this point? Later, when Mengzi set out the transmission of the succession of the Way from Yao and Shun to Tang, he counted Lai Zhu among those who knew it through direct observation. Commentators say, “Lai Zhu was Zhonghui.” This is indeed credible! May those who aspire to the learning of emperors and kings examine this further!

“In summer's heat and rain, the common people do nothing but complain and sigh; in winter's bitter cold, the common people likewise do nothing but complain and sigh. How hard their lot is! Consider their hardships so as to devise means of easing them; then the people will be at peace.”

Zhang Fengchen

…shines brightly within it. It is recorded here as an admonition to those in office.
Associate Examiner Ye, Compiler, comments: The passages recognizing the people's hardships and the duty to provide for them are deeply felt. The writer evidently has given thought to this matter.
Associate Examiner Huang, Compiler, comments: From beginning to end, this composition develops the single word “hardship,” precisely capturing King Mu's intention when he charged Jun Ya with providing for the people.
Associate Examiner Lü, Senior Compiler, comments: Forthright and trustworthy, unadorned and concerned with the people's distress, it brings their suffering vividly before one's eyes. It is enough to stir the reader's compassion for the common people [?].
Examiner Shi, Academician, comments: Here one can still discern the concern for the people shown by the rulers and ministers of the Three Dynasties.
Examiner Jiang, Grand Secretary, comments: Reading this moves one deeply.
The worthy king fully described to his great minister the hardships of the people's livelihood and charged him with addressing them. Whether the people's livelihood is beset by hardship depends simply on how they are provided for. If one knows their hardships but has no means of addressing them, how can one fulfill the responsibility of providing for the people? Long ago, King Mu appointed Jun Ya as Grand Minister of Education. At this point he told him of the difficulty of providing for the people. His meaning was that the people lacked proper provision because those above them did not understand their hardships. “Do you, too, understand the people's hardships?” Thus, summer heat and rain are merely normal features of the seasons. Yet the common people, hampered by lack of food, give voice to resentment and lamentation whenever they encounter summer heat and rain. It is as though they say: “All things have the means to enjoy themselves. Why am I alone unable to do so?” In winter, the bitter cold…

寒而輒發蓋曰物皆有以自適而我何以至此
極也夫人情一日不再食則飢今夏而暑暑而
至於雨民既食有不充其能免於死亡乎終歲
不製衣則寒今冬而寒寒而至於祁民既衣有
不給其能免於窮瘁乎民生之艱信乎其然矣
將何如其處以濟之必也視民之飢猶己飢之
不遑暇食而特為之省憂凡夫溝洫稼穡有關

…is likewise merely part of the regular course of Heaven. Yet the common people, distressed by having no clothing, break into sorrowful sighs when they feel the bitter cold. It is as though they say: “All things have the means to find ease; why have we reached such extremes of misery?” By human nature, people grow hungry if they do not eat twice in a day. Now summer brings heat, and the heat is compounded by rain. Since the people already lack sufficient food, can they escape death? If they make no clothing throughout the year, they suffer cold. Now winter brings cold, and the cold becomes severe. Since the people already lack sufficient clothing, can they escape destitution and exhaustion? The hardships of the people's livelihood are indeed real! How, then, should one address them and bring relief?
One must regard the people's hunger as one's own, allowing oneself no leisure to eat, and give particular attention to their troubles. Everything bearing on food, from irrigation channels to sowing and harvesting, must be managed without daring to omit anything. One must regard the people's cold as one's own, allowing oneself no peaceful rest, and take special thought for them. Everything essential to clothing, from mulberries and hemp to silk and hemp fibre, must be managed without daring to neglect anything. Only then will the hungry obtain food, and worries over summer heat and rain no longer entangle their hearts. Will their complaints then turn into songs rejoicing in life? The cold will obtain clothing, and the suffering of bitter cold will no longer disturb their thoughts. Will their sorrow then turn into joy? The words “then there will be peace” mean that only when things are like this will the people first find peace. Among the difficulties of nourishing the people, none is greater than this! Could Jun Ya fail to devote his whole heart to it?
Yet in the Offices of Zhou, the Minister of Education is responsible for the realm's moral instruction. Why, then, when King Mu appointed Jun Ya, did he charge him instead with nourishing the people? For one first guides them so that their livelihood and sustenance are secured, and then instructs them so that ethical relationships become clear. 福隆夫盛德獲福理之所必然者也詩人託物
以喻之稱頌之誠溢于言表矣昔后妃不妒忌
而子孫衆多為此詩者美之若謂作善降之百

詩人託物以喻后妃，惟逮下之德盛，斯昌後之福隆。夫盛德獲福，理之所必然者也。詩人託物以喻之，稱頌之誠溢于言表矣。昔后妃不妒忌，而子孫衆多，為此詩者美之。若謂作善降之百祥，致福本于一德。以理而論之，人心固足以感乎天；比類而觀之，物性亦可以驗乎人。彼昆蟲之類，物之微者也；螽斯之為物，又昆蟲之微者也。觀其始而動股，繼而振羽，其性若弗靈矣。然亦感至和以並育，恒相聚而不相害焉。作而翔飛，止而跂息，其群宜易渙矣。然亦含大順以有生，每相依而不相違焉。夫物群則爭，而乃詵詵和集如此，由是和以召和，而元化委焉，宜其種類幾于則百之盛；順以達順，而協氣應焉，宜其子孫至于千億之多。生而有滋，滋而有數，以似以續，殆蕃昌而不可計矣。豈大造之賦其形者有所私哉？盖其因有以篤之爾。感而有化，化而無窮，載生載育，殆延綿而不容已矣。豈物稟之

Examiner and Grand Secretary Jiang comments: “The sincerity of loyal devotion overflows beyond the words.”

The poet invokes other creatures to portray the queen consort: only when the virtue of extending benevolence to those below is abundant will the blessing of flourishing descendants be great. That abundant virtue should receive blessings is a necessary consequence of principle. The poet invokes other creatures to convey this, and the sincerity of his praise overflows beyond the words. In former times, the queen consort was free of jealousy and had numerous descendants; the author of this poem praised her for it. It is as though he were saying that a hundred auspicious blessings descend upon those who do good, and that bringing about good fortune is rooted in undivided virtue. Judged by principle, the human heart is indeed capable of moving Heaven; viewed through analogy, the dispositions of other creatures can also furnish evidence concerning human beings.

Insects are insignificant among living things, and katydids are insignificant even among insects. Watching them first move their thighs and then beat their wings, one might think their nature devoid of intelligence. Yet they too respond to the utmost harmony and thrive together, constantly gathering without harming one another. When active, they soar and fly; when still, they perch and rest. Their swarms ought readily to scatter. Yet they too embody supreme accord in their lives, always keeping close to one another without estrangement. Creatures ordinarily contend when they gather, yet these assemble in such abundant harmony. Thus harmony summons harmony, and the primal transforming power of creation bestows itself upon them: fittingly, their kind approaches the abundance expressed by “a hundred.” Accord brings forth accord, and harmonious vital energies respond: fittingly, their descendants reach a thousand or a hundred million in number.

Born, they multiply; multiplying, they grow in number. Continuing and succeeding one another, they flourish almost beyond counting. Could the great creative power that gives them their forms show them special favor? It is simply that the conditions they themselves provide allow it to enrich them. Through responsiveness comes transformation, and transformation knows no end. Bearing and nurturing offspring, they continue almost without possibility of cessation. 同考試官主事薛批：「商人頌美先代之意，是作足以發之，周宜錄矣。」
同考試官給事中夏批：「簡嚴明潔，不類衆作。」
translation_en:
…could what these creatures receive from Heaven really be so exceptional? Surely they themselves have brought this about. Now our queen consort has inherited the virtuous reputation of her predecessors, giving it expression in benevolence extending to those below her. The influence of her harmonious virtue spreads into blessings that make her descendants flourish. With such abundant virtue, it is fitting that she should enjoy such abundant blessings. Can this not also be seen by looking at those locusts? Examining the Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals, we find that the descendants of King Wen in the zhao line and of King Wu in the mu line, together with the offspring of the Duke of Zhou, numbered several dozen branches, all descended from Tai Si. Truly, the multitude of descendants in this dynasty was beyond anything earlier antiquity could match. Yet sacrifices to the god of childbirth and prayers involving bows and bow cases were still recorded in the ritual canons: such was the value they placed on blessed offspring. Ah! When the inner palace is well governed, transformation flourishes in every sphere; when descendants prosper, the foundations of the state are secure. Here this is borne out. The poet used this to praise the queen consort, while the ode praising King Wen likewise says, “He was able to make his descendants flourish.” How, then, could the transforming influence of his example within the family be denied? Let those who later inherit this foundation and legacy look to this.
“Heaven’s command was not departed from; with Tang it reached fulfillment. Tang’s birth was not delayed; his sagely reverence rose daily. His radiant greatness was serene [?]; he revered the Lord on High. Heaven’s command made him a model throughout the nine regions.”
Zhang Heng.
Comment by Associate Examiner Xue, Secretary: “This composition fully brings out the Shang people’s intention in singing the praises of their predecessors. It deserves inclusion [?].”
Comment by Associate Examiner Xia, Supervising Secretary: “Concise, rigorous, lucid, and cleanly written; unlike the other compositions.”

Associate Examiner Wang, a Hanlin Editor, comments: “This composition seems to show an understanding of how difficult it is for Heaven and humanity to enter into mutual accord; therefore I have selected it.”

The sage was born at the proper time and brought his reverence to its utmost perfection: this was how he came to possess All-under-Heaven.
Heaven’s Mandate and the sage’s virtue respond to and move one another. How, then, could Cheng Tang’s possession of All-under-Heaven have been a mere accident? This is why they sang thus at the collective ancestral sacrifice, declaring that the royal enterprise of our Shang had its origins and causes. The auspicious signs of profound wisdom first appeared with King Xuan: was this perhaps the first foundation of Heaven’s Mandate? The allegiance of the regional states grew more extensive under Xiang Tu: was this perhaps a further flourishing of Heaven’s Mandate? By the time of Tang, this mutual accord had endured still longer. The end of one cycle joined the beginning of another, and the glorious course of fortune was renewed. He did not deliberately seek the accomplishment of the royal enterprise; it was as though something opened the way for him. Heaven’s favor and protection were complete, and the succession ordained by Heaven had its appointed recipient. He did not deliberately seek his encounter with Heaven’s Mandate; it was as though something presided over it. title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
時大德昭焉有以懋聖人之敬敬日聖敬功可
已矣而檢飭於身者進進不已方與日而俱升
升曰日升德益至矣而昭假于天者遲遲不息
惟上帝之是畏夫其生也時則天意已有所屬
其敬也至則格天又有其本天其能舍之邪於
是賞以君道使建中以為民極自邦畿暨于要
荒政無所在而不達也責以師道使綏猷以復
民性自王國至于海隅教無所往而不洽也是
則天不苟於立君則其仁天下者大湯不易於
===
===
得天則其有天下也固矣宗廟之祭以是登歌
夫豈不宜抑湯之勉於敬者豈有所利而為哉
天者理之本原即堯舜相授受之中而不可少
易焉者循是而使君子相之則與之合一而罔
不興違是而使小人眩之則謂之棄命而罔不
替後世之君於所謂咸有一德而致思焉當知
所以用力矣
春秋
狄入衛閔公二年 城楚丘僖公二年 吳伐
