時，大德昭焉，有以懋聖人之敬。敬日聖敬，功可已矣，而檢飭於身者進進不已，方與日而俱升。升曰日升，德益至矣，而昭假于天者遲遲不息，惟上帝之是畏。夫其生也時，則天意已有所屬；其敬也至，則格天又有其本。天其能舍之邪？於是賞以君道，使建中以為民極，自邦畿暨于要荒，政無所在而不達也；責以師道，使綏猷以復民性，自王國至于海隅，教無所往而不洽也。是則天不苟於立君，則其仁天下者大；湯不易於得天，則其有天下也固矣。宗廟之祭，以是登歌，夫豈不宜？抑湯之勉於敬者，豈有所利而為哉？天者，理之本原，即堯舜相授受之中，而不可少易焉者。循是而使君子相之，則與之合一而罔不興；違是而使小人眩之，則謂之棄命而罔不替。後世之君，於所謂咸有一德而致思焉，當知所以用力矣。

translation_en:
…the proper time. His great virtue shone forth, enabling him to cultivate a sage’s reverence. His reverence is called “sagely reverence” [?]. His achievement might have sufficed, yet his vigilance and discipline over himself advanced without cease, rising together with the sun. This ascent is called “daily ascent.” His virtue reached ever greater perfection, yet his luminous influence continued steadily to reach Heaven; it was the Lord on High alone whom he held in awe. Since his birth was timely, Heaven’s intent already had its chosen recipient; since his reverence was consummate, his power to move Heaven also had its foundation. How could Heaven forsake him?

Heaven therefore rewarded him with the role of ruler, charging him to establish the mean as the people’s standard. From the royal domain to the distant frontier regions, there was nowhere his government did not reach. It entrusted him with the role of teacher, charging him to bring order to the Way and restore the people’s original nature. From the royal realm to the shores of the seas, there was nowhere his teaching did not permeate. Thus, because Heaven was not careless in establishing a ruler, its benevolence toward all under Heaven was great; because Tang did not easily win Heaven’s favor, his possession of all under Heaven was secure. Was it not fitting that this should be sung in the hall at the ancestral temple sacrifice?

Yet did Tang exert himself in reverence for the sake of any advantage? Heaven is the ultimate source of principle: it is precisely the mean that Yao and Shun transmitted to one another, which cannot be altered in the slightest. If a ruler follows this and has noble men assist him, he becomes one with it and invariably flourishes. If he violates it and lets petty men delude him, this is called abandoning the Mandate, and he invariably declines. If rulers of later ages ponder the saying “all possess a single virtue,” they should understand where to direct their efforts.

Spring and Autumn Annals

…Yue [the thirty-second year of Duke Zhao]; Yuyue entered Wu [the thirteenth year of Duke Ai].
Dai Shibian 戴時弁.
Comment by Associate Examiner Huang, a Hanlin Compiler: “The exposition of how the two rulers strengthened themselves is well shaped and elegantly expressed. It can serve as a model.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Jiang 江, a Hanlin Compiler: “The material is comprehensive [?] and orderly; the language flows freely and has vigor.”
Comment by Examiner Shi, a Hanlin Academician: “It brings out almost the entire meaning of the commentary.”
Comment by Examiner Jiang 蔣, a Grand Secretary: “The reasons why the two rulers passed from adversity to success stand clearly before our eyes.”
The two rulers passed from adversity to success because they grasped the way to strengthen themselves. A ruler who strengthens himself can accomplish things. The resurgence of Wei and Yue indeed arose from this; hence the Spring and Autumn Annals commends them. In former times, the Di watched for an opportunity against Wei, but Wei treated them lightly. Thus duties went unfulfilled at Maoqiu, and disaster culminated at Yingze. Its forces could not prevail, and its people settled at Cao: this was why the lady of Xu composed “Galloping.” Had Duke Wen failed at Teng and Gong [?] and been content to remain an exile, would not the line of Kangshu have fallen? Yet his lack of support stirred his concern, and the scarcity of resources on which he could rely roused his determination. Knowing that ample resources depended on sericulture, he devoted himself to agricultural production [?]; knowing that harmony among the people depended on generosity, he treated merchants and artisans liberally; knowing that the rectification of customs depended on moral transformation, he exalted schooling and instruction; knowing that accomplishing affairs depended on officials, he assessed their aptitudes and abilities. Thus he had thirty chariots in his first year and three hundred in his final year. At the outset, he consulted the oracle…

title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
楚丘之城其終允臧矣於干旄見禮賢之隆焉
於定之方中見勸穡之時焉非秉塞淵之心者
能然乎岐山遷而室家立亶父所以禦狄也衛
其近之不然則是戚施之遺爾將亂之相仍存
可得哉春秋書之蓋予其能復存也吳嘗伐越
越也仇之故釁深于擕李而報逞于夫椒禮幣
行成會稽棲焉國人所為賦飛鳥也使句踐淹
姑蘇而傭隷之安無余之祀其殄乎惟其幽居
以廣志愁形以遠思抱氷懸膽昭其勵也而謀
===
益固蓄陳儲新預其需也而財益紓薄刑省斂
厚其恩也而下益戴審備察聲修其法也而威
alt_text:
楚丘之城其終允臧矣於斯見禮賢之隆焉
於定之方中見勸穡之時焉非秉塞淵之心者
能然乎岐山遷而室家奠父所以禦狄也衛
其近之不然則是戚施之遺爾將亂之相仍存
可得哉春秋書之蓋予其能復存也吳嘗伐越
越也仇之故釁深于檇李而報逞于夫椒禮幣
行成會稽棲焉國人所為賦飛鳥也使句踐遂
姑蘇而備隸之安無余之祀其殄乎惟其幽居
以廣志懸形以遂思抱冰懸膽昭其勵也而謀
===
蓋固著陳儲新預其需也而財蓋紓薄刑省歛
畢其慈也而下蓋戴審備察聲修其法也而威
蓋行是故十年生聚十年教訓遂肆吳郊之入
其更克讐矣於采葛見羽𥜥之華焉於樂辟見
戎殳之利焉非畜堅忍之心者能然乎蠡參謀
而郢都乎包胥所以禦吳也越其類之不然則
是貢獻之邑爾將更之弗遑報可望哉春秋書
之蓋予其能復恥也夫盛衰者勢也強怠者志
也德慧由乎疢疾也全由乎憂患幾也安其志

translation_en:
…the building of the walls at Chuqiu: its eventual outcome was indeed auspicious. In Raised Pennants (Gan mao), we see the lavish respect accorded to worthy men; in When Ding Stood at the Zenith (Ding zhi fang zhong), we see the timely encouragement of agriculture. Could anyone have achieved this without a sincere and profound heart? Danfu moved to Mount Qi and established homes there: this was how he warded off the Di. Wei came close to his example. Otherwise, it would have been merely a legacy of cringing submission [?]; with disorder following upon disorder, could survival have been possible? The Spring and Autumn Annals records this, surely commending Wei’s ability to restore itself and survive.

Wu once attacked Yue, and Yue treated Wu as its enemy. Thus their enmity deepened at Zuili [?], and vengeance was exacted at Fujiao. Yue offered ceremonial gifts and valuables to seek peace and took refuge at Kuaiji. This was why the people of the state composed Flying Birds. Had Goujian lingered at Gusu, content with servitude, would the sacrifices to Wuyu not have been extinguished? Yet in secluded confinement he enlarged his ambitions, and through bodily distress he deepened his deliberations. translation_en:
…By discerning the critical opportunities and refraining from contests of strength, one can pass from adversity to success. Is this why the Spring and Autumn Annals finds something commendable in these two rulers? Even so, when Chu Qiu was walled and the people placed their trust in it, Duke Huan of Qi’s contribution was indeed great. Rather than planning how to meet his state’s troubles, Fuchai devoted his strength to contending for supremacy: he lacked foresight. Guan Zhong was employed, while Wu Yun was executed—was this what brought about their respective outcomes? The Odes says: “The royal kingdom can bring forth men who are the pillars of Zhou.” This speaks of honoring the worthy. It also says: “How is it, vast Heaven, that he will not trust sound counsel?” This speaks of rejecting good advice. Should not those who rule states and houses take warning from this?
“The Son of Heaven sent the Earl of Shao to come and confer a royal mandate upon the duke.” 〔Eighth year of Duke Cheng.〕 “The Earl of Cao returned from the capital.” 〔Sixteenth year of Duke Cheng.〕

Comment by Associate Examiner Huang, Junior Compiler: In the Spring and Autumn period, the rites of Zhou gradually fell into disuse, while punishments and rewards became increasingly disordered. This composition captures particularly well Zhongni’s concern for all under Heaven.
Comment by Associate Examiner Jiang, Junior Compiler: Refined, straightforward, and sound, this differs from compositions that indulge in empty rhetoric. I have therefore selected it.
Comment by Examiner Shi, Academician: It achieves a careful and rigorous style.
Comment by Examiner Jiang, Grand Secretary: Where it discusses the improper bestowal of rewards and failure to impose punishments at that time, its language is stern and its reasoning correct.
The Spring and Autumn Annals records how the royal house favored a prominent state and thereby bestowed rewards improperly, and indulged a small state and thereby failed to impose punishment. Now, governing all under Heaven must begin with punishments and rewards. By conferring a mandate upon Lu and releasing Cao, was Zhou not forfeiting its prospect of recovery?

者象之以制賞而功用丕勸於是乎有圭璧之
錫有袞黻之予有彤弓之貺必覲于闕廷而後
授之故賞不因功非正也成公安於慢而王事
罔舉是謂不共不共者削地又何命焉今遣以
卿士而假以禮辭無乃乖勸乎吾聞賜予之用
外府司之九儀之等宗伯司之策命之出內史
司之先王之賞若斯其慎也及襄之衰猶知恪
===
守府以重備物而簡乃僭焉如天命何春秋特
稱天子而以來賜為文以見魯非往受頒自王
也其亦惜繁纓之意與復國曰歸曹成何以獲
歸簡王釋之也釋諸侯則恩廣矣而謂之失刑
者何曰天有震曜王者象之以制刑而罪用丕
懲於是乎有甲兵之威有斧鉞之誅有刀鋸之
戮必肆諸市朝乃克暴之故刑不加罪非正也
負芻恣於逆而國嗣蒙變是謂不軌不軌者瀦
宮又何歸焉今畀其土田而返其爵位無乃廢

且加策曰何？魯成何以獲命？簡王懷之也。懷諸侯則禮敦矣，而謂之僭賞者何？曰：天有生殖，王者象之以制賞，而功用丕勸。於是乎有圭璧之錫，有袞黻之予，有彤弓之貺，必覲于闕廷而後授之。故賞不因功，非正也。成公安於慢，而王事罔舉，是謂不共。不共者削地，又何命焉？今遣以卿士，而假以禮辭，無乃乖勸乎？吾聞賜予之用，外府司之；九儀之等，宗伯司之；策命之出，內史司之。先王之賞，若斯其慎也。及襄之衰，猶知恪守府，以重備物，而簡乃僭焉，如天命何？《春秋》特稱天子，而以來賜為文，以見魯非往受，頒自王也。其亦惜繁纓之意與？
復國曰歸。曹成何以獲歸？簡王釋之也。釋諸侯則恩廣矣，而謂之失刑者何？曰：天有震曜，王者象之以制刑，而罪用丕懲。於是乎有甲兵之威，有斧鉞之誅，有刀鋸之戮，必肆諸市朝，乃克暴之。故刑不加罪，非正也。負芻恣於逆，而國嗣蒙變，是謂不軌。不軌者瀦宮，又何歸焉？今畀其土田，而返其爵位，無乃廢
translation_en:
…Moreover, why confer a written investiture [?]? How did Duke Cheng of Lu obtain investiture? King Jian cherished him. Cherishing the feudal lords strengthens ritual propriety; why, then, call this an improper reward? The answer is: Heaven gives life and nurture; the king models himself upon it in instituting rewards, thereby greatly encouraging meritorious service. Thus there are gifts of jade tablets and discs, grants of dragon robes and embroidered insignia, and bestowals of vermilion bows. These must be conferred only after an audience at the royal court. Hence rewards that are not based on merit are improper. Duke Cheng was content in his negligence and performed none of his duties to the king. This is called failure to render due service. Those who fail to render due service should have their territory reduced; why, then, invest him? Now the king sends a high minister and favors him with ceremonial words: does this not defeat the purpose of encouragement? I have heard that the resources used for gifts are administered by the Outer Treasury; the gradations of the nine ceremonial protocols, by the Minister of Rites; and the issuing of written investitures, by the Interior Scribe. Such was the care with which the former kings bestowed rewards. Even amid the decline under King Xiang, he still knew to guard the treasury scrupulously, attaching due weight to the full ceremonial regalia. Yet King Jian bestowed rewards improperly. How could this accord with Heaven’s mandate? The Spring and Autumn Annals specifically calls him the ‘Son of Heaven’ and uses the wording ‘came to bestow,’ showing that the ruler of Lu did not go to receive the gift: the bestowal originated with the king. Does this not likewise express the intent to safeguard the privilege of ornamental horse trappings?
Restoration to one’s state is termed ‘return.’ How did Duke Cheng of Cao obtain his return? King Jian released him. Releasing feudal lords extends royal grace; why, then, call this a failure of punishment? The answer is: Heaven has thunder and lightning; the king models himself upon them in instituting punishments, thereby severely chastising wrongdoing. Thus there are the might of armored troops, execution by the battle-axe, and punishment by knife and saw. Punishments must be displayed in the marketplace or at court, so that wrongdoing can be publicly exposed. Hence failure to punish wrongdoing is improper. Fu Chu acted wantonly in rebellion, and the heir to the state suffered calamity. This is called lawlessness. The palace of a lawless man should be razed and its site made into a pool; why, then, allow him to return? Now the king gives him his lands and restores his noble rank: does this not set aside…

愆乎？吾聞立司寇以詰四方，立士師以禁軍國，立訝士以掌獄訟，先王之刑著斯其中也。及穆之耄，猶能訓典獄以明大辟，而簡乃失焉，如天討何？《春秋》不名曹伯，而以歸自為文，以見曹未絕位，宥自王也。其亦謹隕霜之意與？噫！賞僭則陵替之勢成，刑失則放恣之禍長，聖人深有懼焉。經世之慮，不亦深乎？由是觀之，致治在法，行法在正。苟有偏焉，咎之招也。柔偏矣，則賞浮于刑，而人玩之；玩之者削，周是已。剛偏矣，則刑浮于賞，而人怨之；怨之者危，秦是已。《頌》有之：「不剛不柔，敷政優優。」其君天下之要乎？

translation_en:
…offenses? I have heard that Ministers of Justice were established to investigate wrongdoing throughout the realm, Judicial Officers to enforce prohibitions in military and civil affairs, and Judicial Investigators to take charge of criminal cases and litigation. The former kings’ penal principles were embodied in these offices. Even in his old age, King Mu could still instruct those responsible for prisons and clarify the use of capital punishment; yet King Jian failed in this. How could this accord with Heaven’s punishment? The Spring and Autumn Annals does not give the Earl of Cao’s personal name, but uses the wording “returned from” to show that Cao had not been stripped of his rank and that his pardon came from the king. Does this not likewise express the intent of taking care over the descent of frost? Alas! When rewards exceed their proper bounds, a tendency toward the erosion of hierarchy develops; when punishments miscarry, the calamity of unrestrained conduct grows. The Sage was deeply apprehensive about this. Was his concern for ordering the world not profound? Viewed in this light, achieving good government depends on law, and applying law depends on rectitude. Any partiality invites blame. When there is a bias toward leniency, rewards outweigh punishments, and people treat authority lightly. A state whose authority is treated lightly declines: Zhou exemplifies this. When there is a bias toward severity, punishments outweigh rewards, and people resent authority. A state whose authority is resented is endangered: Qin exemplifies this. The Hymns say: “Neither harsh nor soft, he spreads his government with ample ease.” Is this not the essential principle for ruling all under Heaven?
Record of Rites
“The people possess a nature endowed with blood and vital energy, mind and understanding, but have no constant states of sorrow, pleasure, joy, or anger. They respond to stimuli and are stirred into movement by external things; only then do the workings of the heart become manifest.”

The following wording is doubtful: 以叫遂 [?]; the exposition can develop the subject in fine detail…

Human beings possess both nature and feelings; only when feelings are stirred does their nature become manifest. The mind encompasses both nature and feelings. Once feelings are stirred into movement through contact with things, how could the nature harbored within the mind fail to manifest itself outwardly? The author of the Record of Music elaborates on the meaning of how sounds arise, saying that the making of music is rooted in human sounds, and that sounds arise through the stimulation of things. title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
具艴然而怒者亦具也何有常而不變乎及欲
與理之物既感也而人與道之心無不應於喪
所欲之物固哀而得所欲之物則樂也於順其
心之物固喜而逆其心之物則怒也何有感而
不通乎是以心術之原於氣質而為人心者向
固寂然也心術之原於義理而為道心者昔固
渾然也今則形於噍殺嘽緩之聲發於言語而
調於詩歌矣能終隱邪著於發散粗厲之聲繼
之相應而變之成方矣終能藏邪吁音之生本
===
在人心感物如此樂道雖大亦何能外此而興
哉抑論之先王始因人之音以作樂繼又用樂
之音以和人然必人之音皆發於道而安且樂
然後正樂可興此先王之於民所以既以禮樂
刑政同之而又身極和順以聽之無非欲其以
至和之德而興至和之音于以寧四海而官天
地也非兼述作之明聖其孰能與於此
恭儉莊敬而不煩則深於禮者也
方瀾

地也非熹述作之明聖其孰能與於此
恭儉莊敬而不煩則深於禮者也

punctuated:
具，艴然而怒者亦具也。何有常而不變乎？及欲與理之物既感也，而人與道之心無不應。於喪所欲之物固哀，而得所欲之物則樂也；於順其心之物固喜，而逆其心之物則怒也。何有感而不通乎？是以心術之原於氣質而為人心者，向固寂然也；心術之原於義理而為道心者，昔固渾然也。今則形於噍殺嘽緩之聲，發於言語而調於詩歌矣，能終隱邪？著於發散粗厲之聲，繼之相應而變之成方矣，終能藏邪？吁！音之生，本在人心感物如此，樂道雖大，亦何能外此而興哉？抑論之，先王始因人之音以作樂，繼又用樂之音以和人。然必人之音皆發於道而安且樂，然後正樂可興。此先王之於民，所以既以禮樂刑政同之，而又身極和順以聽之，無非欲其以至和之德而興至和之音，于以寧四海而官天地也。非兼述作之明聖，其孰能與於此？

恭儉莊敬而不煩，則深於禮者也。
方瀾
translation_en:
…is present, and so too is indignant anger. How could there be constancy without change? Once things that engage desire and moral principle have made their impact, both the human mind and the mind of the Way invariably respond. Losing what one desires brings sorrow, while obtaining it brings pleasure; encountering what accords with one’s mind brings joy, while encountering what opposes it brings anger. How could there be a stimulus without a corresponding response?

Thus, the workings of the mind that originate in one’s material endowment and constitute the human mind were previously still; those that originate in moral principle and constitute the mind of the Way were previously an undifferentiated whole. Now they take shape in constricted, dwindling sounds or expansive, relaxed ones, finding expression in speech and modulation in poetry and song. Can they remain forever hidden? They become manifest in exuberant, spreading sounds or rough, fierce ones; these follow and answer one another, and their transformations form patterns. Can they remain forever concealed? Ah! The arising of musical sounds is rooted in the human mind’s response to things in this way. Vast though the Way of music may be, how could it arise outside this process?

To pursue the matter further: the former kings first drew upon human vocal sounds to create music, and then used the sounds of music to bring people into harmony. Yet only when people’s sounds all issue from the Way and are peaceful and joyful can correct music flourish. This is why, in dealing with the people, the former kings not only brought them into accord through ritual, music, punishments, and government, but also embodied the utmost harmony and compliance with principle in listening to them. Their sole desire was that the people should, through perfectly harmonious virtue, bring forth perfectly harmonious sounds, thereby bringing peace to all within the Four Seas and ordering Heaven and Earth. Who could participate in this without the luminous sagacity both to transmit and to create?

“To be deferential, frugal, dignified, and reverent without being burdensome is to have a profound understanding of ritual.”
Fang Lan.

得禮之教而無禮之失則其所造也不淺矣盖
===

其深有得於禮教者歟見於經解其旨如此盖

Such is the purport of the passage in “Explanation of the Classics” (Jing jie). …within the bounds of ceremonial rules. They are dignified without the failing of inner weakness [?], and reverent without the fault of affectation or falsity. Thus their dignity and reverence are fitting, without becoming overelaborate amid ritual forms and refinements. To receive the teaching of ritual and apply it without error in this way surely indicates more than a shallow understanding of ritual.

What is within must manifest itself outwardly; steadfast observance proceeds from clear understanding. I know that they have been deeply influenced by the transforming example of those above them: they have standards by which to regulate their conduct, and their deportment naturally becomes solemn and orderly. Surely this is the result of sustained cultivation. They have long received their ruler’s instruction: they have measures by which to restrain themselves, and their bearing naturally becomes gentle and refined. Surely their cultivation has reached maturity. They possess a subtle accord of body and mind, rather than merely knowledge heard and repeated. In their respectfulness and frugality, they have deeply grasped the proper balance of ritual. Could they merely know one aspect and neglect the other? They possess a tacit understanding within their nature and feelings, rather than merely crude outward observances. In their dignity and reverence, they have deeply grasped the correctness of ritual. Could they merely practice its coarse forms and forget its essence?

Thus, practicing ritual is not difficult; avoiding partiality in ritual is difficult. Avoiding partiality in ritual is not difficult; truly apprehending ritual is difficult. Without the profound instruction and transforming influence of the ruler, how could people be brought to embody ritual in this way? Yet this speaks of the results of successful instruction. As for how that instruction is accomplished, this depends upon how those above guide the people. Thus King Wen’s virtue was attested in Yu and Rui, and Confucius’s transforming influence was seen in Zhongdu; the principles of respectfulness, frugality, dignity, and reverence thereby became still clearer. At the end of the Zhou, outward refinement prevailed, almost obliterating substance. translation_en:
…the life-giving principle of the mind is called nature. Thus Zhang Zihou regarded the embodied substance as what fills Heaven and Earth, and nature as what commands Heaven and Earth. This was also Master Cheng’s meaning. Therefore, if the mind can command material force, it can apprehend through personal realization; if it can apprehend in this way, it can fully realize its nature. Thus, by apprehending its embodied substance, it shares in Heaven’s transformations; by fully realizing its nature, it shares in Heaven’s spiritual efficacy. All these are workings of the mind: can it be spoken of as small? When scholars explain the mind solely in terms of what the ears and eyes hear and see, how far are they from equating the mind with the mere square inch of the heart? I obtained this paper late; it comes close to expressing the main outlines of the matter, and so I have included it.
Examiner Shi, Academician, comments: This is precisely Mencius’s teaching of fully realizing one’s mind, knowing one’s nature, and knowing Heaven. Master Cheng points it out to instruct others, making its import still more immediate. This essay elucidates it so thoroughly that scarcely any meaning remains unexplored.
Examiner Jiang, Grand Secretary, comments: Its arguments unfold one after another, yet all are rooted in principle. From this one can judge the author’s self-cultivation.
The sage’s mind is supremely great, and therefore has no separation from Heaven. Only when people themselves diminish their minds do they begin to differ from the sage. Heaven is that from which principle proceeds; the mind is that through which principle is apprehended and personally realized. When principle is fully present, the mind is great. The sage merely preserves intact what is originally so. Thus, nothing in the world is greater than Heaven, and likewise nothing is greater than the sage’s mind. Why is this? Because their principle is indeed a seamless whole, without separation. Only when this principle is not understood do people seek apprehension without employing the mind, seeking it directly in nature instead. Consequently, the doctrine that the mind is small and nature great gains currency, and those in the world who set themselves apart from the sage…

title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
者始衆矣子程子盖有憂之而折諸聖焉斯固
抹世之言也今夫天命流行生生弗息四德之
善迭相繼也二氣之行迭相乘也五行之用迭
相成也生殖震曜迭相化也萬殊百慮何莫而
非原於天者乎故曰天者理之所自出者也氣
與形合而人生焉理與氣合而心具焉寂而感
近而遠微而著是心之妙也故其動也是即鼓
萬物之出機而顯諸仁也其靜也是即鼓萬物
之入機而藏諸用也用固與天同流而體則與
===
天同其大備萬物貫萬事非心孰為之故曰心
也者理之所由以體會者也聖人踐形而肖乎
天天體物而不遺聖人之心則體事而無不在
推之使出而達道行焉用之妙也斂之使入而
大本立焉體斯具矣故曰聖人全其心之本然
者也仁義禮智與四德一也時靜時動與二氣
一也卷舒運用與五行一也喜以物之當喜怒
以物之當怒與生殖震曜一也而凡寂感近遠
微著以達于萬變莫不皆然盖其體與天同無

punctuated: 者始衆矣。子程子盖有憂之，而折諸聖焉，斯固抹世之言也。今夫天命流行，生生弗息，四德之善迭相繼也，二氣之行迭相乘也，五行之用迭相成也，生殖震曜迭相化也。萬殊百慮，何莫而非原於天者乎？故曰：「天者，理之所自出者也。」氣與形合而人生焉，理與氣合而心具焉。寂而感，近而遠，微而著，是心之妙也。故其動也，是即鼓萬物之出機而顯諸仁也；其靜也，是即鼓萬物之入機而藏諸用也。用固與天同流，而體則與天同其大。備萬物，貫萬事，非心孰為之？故曰：「心也者，理之所由以體會者也。」聖人踐形而肖乎天。天體物而不遺，聖人之心則體事而無不在。推之使出而達道行焉，用之妙也；斂之使入而大本立焉，體斯具矣。故曰：「聖人全其心之本然者也。」仁義禮智，與四德一也；時靜時動，與二氣一也；卷舒運用，與五行一也；喜以物之當喜，怒以物之當怒，與生殖震曜一也。而凡寂感近遠微著，以達于萬變，莫不皆然。盖其體與天同無
translation_en: …those who set themselves apart from the sages thus began to multiply. Master Cheng was evidently troubled by this and adjudicated the matter by reference to the sages. These are indeed words to instruct the age [?]. Now Heaven’s mandate flows onward, generating life without cease. The goodness of the four virtues succeeds in turn; the operations of the two vital forces follow upon one another; the functions of the Five Phases complete one another; and generation, growth, shaking, and illumination transform into one another. Of the myriad differences and hundred concerns, which does not originate in Heaven? Thus it is said: “Heaven is that from which principle issues.” When vital force joins with physical form, human beings are born; when principle joins with vital force, the mind is fully constituted. Still yet responsive, near yet far-reaching, subtle yet manifest—such is the wondrous working of the mind. In its activity, it sets in motion the outward workings of the myriad things and manifests itself in humaneness; in its stillness, it sets in motion their inward workings and conceals itself in functioning. Its functioning indeed flows together with Heaven, while its substance shares Heaven’s greatness. Encompassing the myriad things and pervading all affairs—what but the mind could do this? Thus it is said: “The mind is that through which principle is apprehended and embodied.” The sage fulfills his bodily form and thereby resembles Heaven. Heaven embodies all things without omission; the sage’s mind embodies affairs and is present in all of them. When extended outward, the universally accessible Way proceeds: this is the wondrous character of its functioning. When gathered inward, the great foundation is established: its substance is thereby complete. Thus it is said: “The sage preserves intact the original condition of his mind.” Humaneness, righteousness, ritual propriety, and wisdom are one with the four virtues of Heaven; stillness and activity, each in its proper time, are one with the two vital forces; contraction, expansion, operation, and application are one with the Five Phases; rejoicing at what warrants joy and becoming angry at what warrants anger are one with generation, growth, shaking, and illumination. Stillness and responsiveness, nearness and distance, subtlety and manifestation, extending to the myriad transformations—all are thus. For its substance, like Heaven’s, is without …

title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
限量而用則與天相為流通矣故曰其理固渾
然而無間也夫天下之理體會必以心非心則
無從而體會之章章明也人惟滯心于智識之
間則心之本然者不可得而見顧曰心小性大
而不知性統於心者也能大其心則萬理畢具
而成性自此而存苟小其心則其本體有所不
盡而蔽於物并其性而梏亡之矣異端之所以
悖吾道者實源于此故曰人自小之始與聖人
異也抑詩曰維天之命於穆不已於乎不顯文
===
王之德之純文王之所以合天道者小心翼翼
其作聖之功也然則心小之云亦豈無所見哉
蓋文王之小心焉者自持以敬存其心者也異
端之以心為小者自私用智遺其心者也持敬
則真積久真積久則體會深而吾心之所契者
非人而忽天非人而忽天則前乎開闢而未嘗
古也後乎開闢而未嘗今也其在我者即其在
於聖人者也是則心之為妙從事於學則小而
敬復其本然則大而通也斯民也先哲固嘗本

於聖人者也是則心之爲妙從事於學則小而

punctuated: 限量，而用則與天相為流通矣。故曰：「其理固渾然而無間也。」夫天下之理，體會必以心，非心則無從而體會之，章章明也。人惟滯心于智識之間，則心之本然者不可得而見，顧曰心小性大，而不知性統於心者也。能大其心，則萬理畢具，而成性自此而存；苟小其心，則其本體有所不盡，而蔽於物，并其性而梏亡之矣。異端之所以悖吾道者，實源于此。故曰：「人自小之，始與聖人異也。」抑《詩》曰：「維天之命，於穆不已！於乎不顯，文王之德之純！」文王之所以合天道者，小心翼翼，其作聖之功也。然則心小之云，亦豈無所見哉？蓋文王之小心焉者，自持以敬，存其心者也；異端之以心為小者，自私用智，遺其心者也。持敬則真積久，真積久則體會深，而吾心之所契者，非人而忽天。非人而忽天，則前乎開闢而未嘗古也，後乎開闢而未嘗今也。其在我者，即其在於聖人者也。是則心之為妙，從事於學則小而敬，復其本然則大而通也。斯民也，先哲固嘗本
translation_en:
…without limit, while in its functioning it flows in mutual communion with Heaven. Thus it is said: “Its principle is indeed an undivided whole, without any separation.” That the principles of all under Heaven must be comprehended through the mind, and that without the mind there is no means of comprehending them, is perfectly clear. Yet people confine their minds within intellectual knowledge, so that the mind’s original condition can no longer be seen. They nevertheless say that the mind is small and human nature great, not knowing that human nature is encompassed by the mind. If one can enlarge one’s mind, all principles will be fully present, and one’s fully realized nature will thereby be preserved. If, however, one makes one’s mind small, its fundamental substance will not be fully realized; obscured by things, one will fetter and destroy even one’s own nature. This is truly the source of heterodox teachings’ opposition to our Way. Thus it is said: “Only when people diminish it themselves do they begin to differ from the sages.”
Moreover, the Book of Odes says: “The mandate of Heaven—how profound and unceasing! Ah, how illustrious was the purity of King Wen’s virtue!” What enabled King Wen to accord with the Way of Heaven was his cautious reverence: this was the effort through which he became a sage. Can speaking of a ‘small mind,’ then, be entirely without insight? King Wen’s cautiousness meant governing himself with reverence and preserving his mind. The heterodox view that the mind is small means employing cleverness for selfish ends and abandoning the mind. Maintaining reverence allows genuine effort to accumulate over time; as it accumulates, comprehension deepens, and what our mind accords with is ‘not human but suddenly Heaven’ [?]. Being ‘not human but suddenly Heaven’ [?], it precedes the opening of Heaven and Earth yet is never ancient; it follows that opening yet is never modern. What is present in me is precisely what is present in the sages. Such is the subtle efficacy of the mind: in pursuing learning, it is small and reverent; restored to its original condition, it is great and all-pervading. For these people, earlier worthies had indeed once drawn upon …

子程子之意言之矣，曰：「心生道也，敬者心之所以生也。」

同前。陳褒。

同考試官主事唐批：孔門自子貢言性與天道後，子思發之以天命謂性，孟子繼之以存養事天，則心與天為一之理大明矣。此卷因程子體會之說，再千餘言，翻疊聖人心性許多理致，出示意知乎錄，非但可聞夫子文章而已。

translation_en:
…expressed Master Cheng’s meaning, saying: “The heart gives life to the Way; reverence is that by which the heart lives.”

Same topic as above. By Chen Bao.

Comment by Associate Examiner Tang, Secretary: Within the school of Confucius, after Zigong spoke of human nature and the Way of Heaven, Zisi elucidated this through the statement that what Heaven commands is called human nature. Mencius continued it through preserving the heart, nourishing one’s nature, and serving Heaven. Thus the principle that the heart and Heaven are one became abundantly clear. Taking up Master Cheng’s explanation of inward comprehension, this paper, in a further thousand or more words [?], unfolds layer upon layer of the many principles concerning the sage’s heart and nature. It sets forth the meaning [remainder of phrase unclear: 出示意知乎錄, ?]; it allows one to hear more than merely the Master’s cultured teachings.

Comment by Associate Examiner Sun, Compiler: Human nature, the heart, and Heaven share a single principle. The sage fully realizes his nature and can inwardly comprehend the principles of all under Heaven; hence he is one with Heaven. Scholars have not spoken of this with sufficient precision. You have conveyed its meaning through your brush, and its pointed brilliance presses forcefully upon the reader [羞羞 unclear, ?]. In composing an essay, clarifying the heart is the foundation, and nourishing vital energy is the aid. You have attained both. Reading this, I feel truly compelled to straighten my robes in respect.

Comment by Examiner Shi, Academician: The discussion of principle is exceptionally refined. At the end, he returns to abiding in reverence as the starting point for learning to become a sage. He comes close to understanding how one advances from learning below to comprehension above.

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Grand Secretary: The analysis of principle is refined and profound, and the writing fluent and lucid. An outstanding work among the discourses in this examination [one illegible character].

title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
論曰天下無心外之理也聖人之心不遺乎理
則不異於天矣夫性乃心之所具之理心之能
體性猶天之能體物也天體物而不遺心亦體
性而不遺也惟夫梏於見聞之小而不能體性
於心於是心小性大而天下之理遺於此心之
外者多矣若是而謂之與天為一可乎夫惟聖
人之心包涵天下之理而不遺故性全於心心
全於天天大無外而聖人之心亦大而無外也
程子曰聖人之心與天為一所謂與天為一者
===
正以其心能體會乎性焉耳請申其說天地之

The discourse reads: There is no principle under Heaven outside the mind. Since the sage’s mind leaves no principle unembraced, it is no different from Heaven. Human nature is the principle inherent in the mind. The mind’s capacity to embody human nature is like Heaven’s capacity to embody things. Heaven embodies things without omission; the mind likewise embodies human nature without omission. Only when people are confined by the narrowness of what they have seen and heard, and cannot embody human nature in their minds, does the mind become small while human nature remains vast. Much of the principle under Heaven is then left outside this mind. Can such a mind be called one with Heaven? The sage’s mind alone embraces all principle under Heaven without omission. Thus human nature is complete in the mind, and the mind is complete in Heaven. Heaven is so vast that nothing lies outside it; the sage’s mind is likewise so vast that nothing lies outside it. Master Cheng said: “The sage’s mind is one with Heaven.” What is meant by being one with Heaven is precisely that his mind can embody and comprehend human nature.

Let me elaborate. Among beings endowed with a nature by Heaven and Earth, humans are the most precious. What makes humans precious is their mind. In its functioning, the mind dwells in benevolence, stores itself in righteousness, acts through ritual propriety, knows through wisdom, and brings things to completion through trustworthiness. Through these it forms a triad with Heaven and Earth, illumines the sun and moon, orders the four seasons, sets the mountains firmly in place, makes rivers and seas flow, and causes grasses and trees to flourish. All principle under Heaven—above and below, hidden and manifest, ending and beginning, death and life, transformation and spirits—is invariably where human nature resides, and thus invariably falls within the mind’s compass. Although this mind governs a single body, the emptiness and numinous awareness of its substance suffice to contain all principle under Heaven. 心異人而夫人之非聖人者亦不能以其心異
聖人聖人也心也天也較然一也夫人能知之
而程子獨為此言何哉蓋心雖天下之所同而
性則非天下之所同體人之心雖同於聖人而
其體會此性於心者則不能皆聖人也故有以
非聞不足以盡心而極力於其所聞以非見不

…one with Heaven, while Heaven has never been other than one with humanity. Thus even a sage cannot have a mind different from that of other people, and those who are not sages likewise cannot have minds different from a sage’s. The sage, the mind, and Heaven are manifestly one. Everyone can know this; why, then, did Master Cheng alone make this statement? Although the mind is common to all under Heaven, not everyone equally embodies the nature. Although people’s minds are the same as those of sages, they cannot all be sages in their realization of this nature within their minds. Hence some think that without hearing they cannot fully realize the mind, and devote all their efforts to what they hear; others think that without seeing they cannot fully realize the mind, and devote all their efforts to what they see. Alas! Can the mind really be exhausted by hearing and seeing? If it could, the mind within a person would indeed be small. Yet the mind is fundamentally not small. Thus, to devote all one’s efforts to what one hears is to be fettered by what one hears, so that whatever lies beyond one’s hearing becomes something the mind cannot hear. To devote all one’s efforts to what one sees is to be fettered by what one sees, so that whatever lies beyond one’s sight becomes something the mind cannot see. Once the mind cannot see and hear these things, the nature cannot be fully realized; once the nature cannot be fully realized, unity with Heaven cannot be attained. Alas! Could anyone suppose that the mind of a sage is like this?

Moreover, what sort of mind is the sage’s mind? As the nature exists throughout the world, nothing can lie outside it; and as the mind exists within the sage, even the nature cannot lie outside it. Thus, the account of the hidden and the manifest is a domain in which the nature resides. The sage looks upward and examines downward, and thereby comes to know the reasons for the hidden and the manifest. Knowing the hidden…

The sage traces things to their beginnings and returns to their ends, thereby coming to understand the explanation of death and life. Understanding this, he holds within his mind the nature present in death and life. The dispositions and forms of ghosts and spirits are a locus of nature. The sage observes changes and things, thereby coming to understand the dispositions and forms of ghosts and spirits. Understanding these, he holds within his mind the nature present in ghosts and spirits. Extending even to the transformations of Heaven and Earth, this mind encompasses them without overstepping; it brings the principles of the myriad things to fulfillment in all their particulars, omitting none; it penetrates the Way of day and night and knows it completely. Thus, when benevolence is embodied in the mind, one can become one with Heaven’s origination; when righteousness is embodied in the mind, one can become one with Heaven’s benefit; when ritual propriety and wisdom are embodied in the mind, one can become one with Heaven’s flourishing and constancy; when trustworthiness is embodied in the mind, one can become one with Heaven’s sincerity, unity, and absence of duplicity. 一乾元之變化而已易曰先天而天弗違中庸
曰浩浩其天盖謂此也所以然者盖理之在天
下也不外於其心而心之在聖人也不遺乎其
理此其所以與天為一也歟向使聖人之心猶
有未體會於其理而天下之理猶有外於聖人

一乾元之變化而已。《易》曰：「先天而天弗違。」《中庸》曰：「浩浩其天。」盖謂此也。所以然者，盖理之在天下也，不外於其心；而心之在聖人也，不遺乎其理。此其所以與天為一也歟？向使聖人之心猶有未體會於其理，而天下之理猶有外於聖人之心，則偏狹固滯，雖欲其不自小，不可得矣，而尚望其與天為一乎？雖然，初非天賦以是心而獨使之與天為一也，其初盖出於天下之所同而已矣。出於天下之所同，而天下不能以自大其心，於是乎始有天人之别。使夫人而能體會其性於心，則其與天為一也，亦奚殊哉？使聖人之心而不體會乎性，吾亦不知果能與天為一否也。孔子曰：「十室之邑，必有忠信如丘者焉，不如丘之好學也。」嗚呼！幸而有資如聖人矣，而卒不如聖人之好學，果將安咎哉？然則學者之欲大其心者，當何如？亦惟自格物致知始。

translation_en:
…are all simply transformations of the originating power of Qian, the Creative. The Book of Changes says, “He precedes Heaven, yet Heaven does not go against him.” The Doctrine of the Mean says, “Vast, vast is his Heaven.” These surely refer to this. The reason is that the principles throughout the world do not lie outside the sage’s mind, while the sage’s mind omits none of those principles. Is this not why he is one with Heaven? Suppose the sage’s mind had still failed to apprehend some of these principles, and some principles in the world still lay outside his mind. Then he would be narrow, confined, rigid, and obstructed: even if he wished to avoid diminishing himself, he could not do so. How could one still expect him to be one with Heaven?

Nevertheless, it was not that Heaven originally endowed him with this mind so that he alone might be one with Heaven. At the outset, it surely arose only from what all people share. Yet although it arose from what all share, people cannot themselves enlarge their minds; only then does the distinction between Heaven and humanity arise. If everyone could apprehend their nature within their mind, how would their oneness with Heaven be any different? If the sage’s mind did not apprehend human nature, I too would not know whether he could truly be one with Heaven. Confucius said, “In a settlement of ten households, there are sure to be people as loyal and trustworthy as I, Qiu, but none as fond of learning as I.” Alas! Fortunate enough to possess endowments like those of the sage, yet ultimately failing to equal his love of learning—where, indeed, could one lay the blame? What, then, should learners who wish to enlarge their minds do? They must simply begin by investigating things and extending knowledge.

Associate Examiner Xue, Bureau Secretary, comments: “The language is plain and substantial, and the sentiments earnest and sincere. Should a memorial not be like this?”

Associate Examiner Xia, Supervising Secretary, comments: “Writing that eschews parallel phrasing yet has a full and substantial style: this is indeed an excellent memorial.”

Associate Examiner Chen, Compiler, comments: “It does not prize ornate language. Might the author be intent upon classical standards? It should be recorded as a model.”

Associate Examiner Wang, Compiler, comments: “The genuine benevolence and concern for the people shared by the ruler and his ministers at that time can still be envisaged.”

Associate Examiner Yang, Senior Compiler, comments: “The memorial is free of labored embellishment; its author evidently does not concentrate solely on wording.”

On a certain day of a certain month in a certain year, we reverently received an imperial edict instructing us, Your servants, to exercise reverent care and compassion in penal matters. We humbly reflect that, in this season of oppressive heat, Your Majesty remains unwearied by anxious toil. Your heart is troubled for those held in prison, and Your benevolent intentions have thus found expression in this proclamation…

translation_en:
…Your grace reaches first those in prison, and rejoicing overflows throughout the realm. Your servants, So-and-so and the others, are truly joyful and delighted; we bow our heads to the ground and kowtow.
We humbly reflect that when representations of punishments were displayed at the court of Yu, particular importance was attached to reverent concern; when penalties were set forth in the proclamations of Zhou, the difficulty of exercising due caution was explained in detail. A king’s just administration of punishments bears upon the very lives of his people. Although the prohibitions of the statutes serve to warn the wicked and recalcitrant, the people, like innocent children, lack understanding: it is especially necessary to distinguish deliberate offenses from inadvertent ones. Compassion for suffering that cuts to the skin must lead to reductions in punishments of shaving the head and tattooing. Inspired by the banner inviting good counsel, one should show leniency toward critical speech. Moreover, when inadvertent offenses and misfortunes occur, their root lies in inadequate moral instruction and guidance. If awesome severity is applied on a great scale, the people’s simple, generous character will surely be gradually eroded. Should the people rise in disobedience and resentment, the ruler himself must feel their suffering keenly.
Now we have humbly encountered [four circle marks in the text: 〇〇〇〇; imperial designation omitted?] whose sagacity and wisdom are innate, whose magnanimity is Heaven-bestowed. Embodying Heaven’s creative power, you preserve harmony; thereby you adorn enlightened civilization. Your virtue equals that of Tang of Yin: your benevolence is repeatedly manifested in the spirit of his prayer over the hunting nets. Your Way accords with that of Yu of Xia: your compassion is no different from his weeping over an offender. Mindful that the prisons are not yet empty, you feel still greater concern amid the oppressive summer heat. In a single document you issue the ten lines of…

詔，片言回四海之春。語實出於由衷，惠常行於法外。銜慍者應薫風而即解，病暍者望甘雨以先甦。德意敷山東，羣黎思化；璽書下河右，萬里歸明。馨香上徹于兩間，和氣旁流于四海。臣等敢不躬常佩夫綸綍，訟期息於閭閻，祗率庶僚，奉揚耿命。無胥戕，無胥虐，惟貌有稽；至于再，至于三，得情勿喜。遠慕蘇公之敬，聿追定國之平。伏願體好生之德，廣皇心，以君子之道待天下，民命咸躋於仁壽，國脉益衍於延長。臣等下情無任瞻天仰聖、欣躍感戴之至，謹奉表稱謝以聞。

第叁場
translation_en:
…edict; a few words restore spring throughout the realm. Your words truly issue from the heart, and your favors often extend beyond the provisions of the law. Those harboring resentment feel it immediately dissolve at the coming of the balmy wind; those suffering from oppressive heat revive even as they await the welcome rain. Your virtuous intentions spread through Shandong, and the common people yearn for transformation. Your sealed letter descends upon Heyou, and people ten thousand li away turn toward your enlightened rule. Its fragrance rises through heaven and earth, and harmonious influences spread throughout the realm.

How could we, your servants, fail always to cherish your imperial words, seeking to end litigation among the people, respectfully leading the assembled officials, and upholding and proclaiming your illustrious command? Let none injure one another or abuse one another; let their demeanor be examined [?]. Review cases a second and a third time, and take no pleasure in discovering the facts of an offense. We look far back in admiration to the reverence of Su Gong and strive to emulate Dingguo’s impartiality.

We humbly wish that you embody the virtue of cherishing life, broaden your imperial benevolence, and treat all under Heaven according to the way of the gentleman, so that all the people may enjoy humane rule and long life, and the dynasty’s vitality may endure ever longer. Gazing toward Heaven and looking up to Your Sagely Majesty, we, your servants, cannot contain our profound joy, gratitude, and devotion. We respectfully submit this memorial to express our thanks for your hearing.

Third Session

策。第一問。李舜臣。

同考試官給事中趙批：我聖祖開國啓後之仁，多士率能道之，第少見對揚有據者。子獨述之眞切，抑可謂識其大矣。矧諸作俱學識不群，而逸氣俊才於渾融中自著，髙薦何疑？

同考試官編修葉批：初中二塲，已讓子出一頭地。及得五策，如瑶瑜入手，雖彞琥琮璜，而晶光渾沁，不𢩁華暴，令人把玩不置。此昌運所鍾，非偶然者。首篇陳聖祖事尤善，錄之固宜。

同考試官編修黃批：之爲士，志與學而已。此卷初中二塲，已知邃密之學；五策經綸規模，反復數千言，占知有志於天下者。首策以仁爲主，尤足以揄揚我聖祖開基詒謀之至意。嗣是而闡伊尹之志，光輔熈朝，以仁天下，不有望耶？
translation_en:
Policy Essays. First Question. Li Shunchen.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Supervising Secretary: Most candidates can speak of the benevolence with which our Sagely Progenitor founded the dynasty and provided for posterity, but few offer a substantiated exposition that fittingly extols it. You alone describe it with truth and precision, and may indeed be said to grasp its essential greatness. Moreover, all your compositions display exceptional learning and insight; an untrammeled spirit and outstanding talent reveal themselves naturally within their harmonious wholeness. What doubt can there be about recommending you highly?

Comment by Associate Examiner Ye, Compiler: The first and second sessions had already placed you a head above the others. On receiving your five policy essays, I felt as though fine jade had come into my hands. Whether ritual vessels, tiger-shaped jades, cong tubes, or huang pendants, their crystalline radiance permeates the whole, without garish display [?], inviting one to handle and admire them without setting them down. Here the auspicious fortunes of the age have concentrated their gifts; this is no accident. The first essay is especially fine in its account of the Sagely Progenitor’s deeds. It is certainly fitting to include it in the record.

Comment by Associate Examiner Huang, Compiler: To be a scholar [?] is simply a matter of aspiration and learning. From this candidate’s papers in the first and second sessions, one could already recognize profound and meticulous learning. The five policy essays elaborate plans for ordering the realm over several thousand words, showing [?] that he has aspirations for All-under-Heaven. The first essay takes benevolence as its central theme and is especially well suited to extolling the deepest intent of our Sagely Progenitor in laying the dynasty’s foundations and bequeathing plans to posterity. May we not hope that henceforth he will give fuller expression to Yi Yin’s aspirations, lend illustrious assistance to our flourishing dynasty, and bring benevolence to All-under-Heaven?

title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
同考試官修撰呂批寬仁以救民而發政
雖或極刑惡逆亦為民耳此我
聖祖開國永世之至意也一時賢佐忠厚之論亦與有采焉士能
反復辯著其蘊而徵諸天地之大德足為
今日獻矣且諸策若於審是論道學知燔書之設難以救時論
寬猛悉慢殘之隱情蓋皆即寬仁忠厚而發之
士子識時務尚有如此者乎且前二場主司又
皆共諒其有積養也天下之選無以踰子矣
考試官學士石批五策議論辯博卓有
===
定見而詞氣渾然不露鋒鍔天下之奇才也
考試官大學士蔣批此卷前二場俱優五
策隨問隨答略無凝滯而詞氣超然脫塵離俗
敻出筆墨畦徑之外深博之學奇特之才昌大
之氣具見於文字間而此答尤偉
龍飛初科得斯士褒然舉首足以為科目之光矣
聖人創鴻業而繫萬國之心詒燕謀而周
萬世之慮無他道焉仁而已矣蓋人情莫
不好生而聖人之仁又天下所恃以為命

punctuated:
同考試官修撰呂批：寬仁以救民而發政，雖或極刑惡逆，亦為民耳。此我聖祖開國永世之至意也。一時賢佐忠厚之論，亦與有采焉。士能反復辯著其蘊，而徵諸天地之大德，足為今日獻矣。且諸策，若於審是論道學，知燔書之設難以救時；論寬猛，悉慢殘之隱情，蓋皆即寬仁忠厚而發之。士子識時務，尚有如此者乎？且前二場主司又皆共諒其有積養也。天下之選，無以踰子矣。
考試官學士石批：五策議論辯博，卓有定見，而詞氣渾然，不露鋒鍔，天下之奇才也。
考試官大學士蔣批：此卷前二場俱優，五策隨問隨答，略無凝滯，而詞氣超然，脫塵離俗，敻出筆墨畦徑之外。深博之學、奇特之才、昌大之氣，具見於文字間，而此答尤偉。龍飛初科，得斯士褒然舉首，足以為科目之光矣。
聖人創鴻業而繫萬國之心，詒燕謀而周萬世之慮，無他道焉，仁而已矣。蓋人情莫不好生，而聖人之仁，又天下所恃以為命
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Lü, Senior Compiler, comments: Government is instituted with magnanimity and benevolence to save the people. Even when the most severe punishments are imposed upon the wicked and rebellious, this too is for the people’s sake. Such was the deepest intention of our Sagely Progenitor in founding the state and securing its perpetuity. The generous and considerate counsels of the worthy ministers of that time also contributed something of value. This candidate repeatedly elucidates their underlying meaning through argument and corroborates it by reference to the great virtue of Heaven and Earth. His work is worthy of being offered to the present age. Moreover, in the various policy essays—for example, in examining what is right and discussing the Learning of the Way [?], he understands the objection posed concerning book-burning as intended to remedy the troubles of the time; in discussing leniency and severity, he fully understands the underlying circumstances of laxity and cruelty. All these arguments proceed from magnanimity, benevolence, generosity, and consideration. Are there still candidates with such an understanding of the affairs of the age? Furthermore, the examiners in charge of the first two sessions all recognized his accumulated learning and cultivation. Among those selected throughout the realm, none can surpass you.
Examiner Shi, Academician, comments: The arguments in these five policy essays are wide-ranging and discriminating, displaying outstandingly firm judgments. Yet their language and spirit form a harmonious whole, revealing no sharp edges. This is an exceptional talent of the realm.
Examiner Jiang, Grand Secretary, comments: This candidate’s papers in the first two sessions were both excellent. In the five policy essays, he answers each question as it comes, without the slightest hesitation or impediment. His language and spirit rise above the ordinary, free of worldly dust and vulgarity, reaching far beyond the conventional paths of literary composition. Profound and extensive learning, exceptional talent, and an expansive spirit are all evident in his writing, and this answer is especially magnificent. To discover such a scholar in the first examination following the Emperor’s accession, and to acclaim him as foremost, is enough to bring glory to the examination system.
When the sage establishes his great enterprise and binds to himself the hearts of the myriad states, and bequeaths plans for his descendants’ security while taking thought comprehensively for ten thousand generations, there is no other way: it is benevolence alone. For human nature invariably cherishes life, and the sage’s benevolence is also what all under Heaven depend upon for their very existence…

title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
者愛之也如父母則其歸我也如流水是
所謂純王之道也創業詒謀其有能易此
者乎歷觀前代皆未有如我
聖祖高皇帝之盛者也

…If he loves them as parents do, they will turn to him like flowing water. This is what is called the way of pure kingly rule. In founding a dynasty and bequeathing plans to posterity, could anyone depart from this? Surveying successive earlier dynasties, none attained the greatness of our Sagely Progenitor, Emperor Gao. His divine designs and mighty achievements are so vast as to defy description. How could someone as ignorant as I adequately comprehend them? Yet, prompted by your discerning question, I venture to portray one ten-thousandth of them and seek your correction, sir.

What made the Sagely Progenitor a true ruler is precisely what makes Heaven Heaven. Only after understanding what makes Heaven Heaven can one comprehend the Sagely Progenitor’s heart. Why is this? Benevolence is the life-giving heart of Heaven and Earth, through which human beings obtain life. Thus it is said, “All people have a heart that cannot bear the suffering of others.” It is also said, “The originating power is foremost among goodness.” Bringing forth living things in spring is Heaven’s benevolence; subjecting them to autumn’s severity is also Heaven’s benevolence. Activity and stillness are each the root of the other; yin and yang each work wondrously in their respective functions. The sage embodies this. Thus, through kindness and harmony he models himself on spring’s generation of life, and through punishments he models himself on autumn’s severity. In everything he does there is benevolence. Yet yang regularly occupies midsummer, taking growth and nourishment as its task, while yin regularly accumulates in the depths of winter, in places empty and unused. Hence, taking no pleasure in killing people is especially expressive of the sage’s original heart. translation_en: …the Sagely Founder arose: truly Heaven mandated him to bring peace to the people of All under Heaven. His heart, which took no pleasure in killing, was already sincere and generous by nature, and was further cultivated and illuminated through learning. Like spring in its relation to living things, he benefited them daily without either being conscious of it. Why should he have needed another’s words before being moved? Yet, when he first crossed the Yangzi, he approved of Tao An’s words upon reaching Gushu, and delighted in Song Lian’s response upon reaching Jinling. At Xin’an he invited and consulted the elders; as soon as he heard Tang Zhongshi discuss the way to pacify and unify All under Heaven, he bestowed generous rewards upon him and offered him comfort. This was the magnanimous heart of Yao and Shun, who shared with others in doing good. At that time, when he campaigned in the east, those in the west lamented that he had not come to them. His awe-inspiring fame spread far to the edges of the seas; the great feared him and the small cherished him, and his glorious achievements reached throughout Heaven and Earth. Truly, as a worthy predecessor said, “The people’s lives were duly fulfilled, and all living things flourished.” All this was the work of his consummate benevolence alone. punctuated: 聖人在上，轉移之際，丰采頓殊。而大亂之後，民無定志，不有嚴法，何以懾其心而驅之于仁義禮樂之域？此《大誥》之所由作也。仁義並行，恩威不爽，舒卷操縱，至神莫測，而何病于安天下之初心哉？至于《祖訓》一書，紬繹六年，始克成編，其為聖子神孫慮者重以周矣。而嚴法繩下之戒尤亹亹焉，且深戒臣下毋或輒啟威虐，以輔我國家億萬年渾厚淳龐之治。蓋立法不可不嚴，而其詒謀也不可不仁。惟其立法之嚴也，故足以震疊一時豪傑，使潛消其異志；惟其詒謀以仁也，故聖子神孫有所監視持循，益培養國脉以至于厚，則天下之人心益固結而不可解。嗚呼！此又聖祖所以周萬世之慮者也。昔蘇轍氏論一天
translation_en:
…with the sage upon the throne, the tenor of the age changed abruptly in the transition. Yet after great disorder, the people had no settled purpose. Without strict laws, how could he overawe their hearts and lead them into the realm of benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music? This was why the Grand Pronouncements (Da Gao) was composed. Benevolence and righteousness operated together; favor and severity were duly apportioned. His relaxation and tightening of control were so wondrous as to be unfathomable. How could this have compromised his original intention to bring peace to the realm?

As for the Ancestral Instructions (Zuxun), only after six years of careful elaboration was the book completed. His concern for his sagely sons and divine grandsons was weighty and comprehensive. He was especially tireless in warning against using harsh laws to keep subordinates in check, and he earnestly admonished his ministers never rashly to initiate coercion and cruelty, thereby sustaining for countless ages the generous, sincere, and unspoiled governance of our dynasty. For legislation must be strict, but the plans bequeathed to posterity must be benevolent. Precisely because his legislation was strict, it could overawe the powerful men of his age and quietly extinguish their disloyal ambitions. Precisely because his plans for posterity were benevolent, his sagely sons and divine grandsons had something to consult and follow, further nourishing the dynasty’s vitality until its foundations grew substantial. Thus the allegiance of all the people in the realm became ever firmer and could not be undone. Ah! This, too, was how the sagely founder took comprehensive thought for ten thousand generations. Formerly, Su Zhe discussed those who unified the realm…

punctuated:
下者四君，而執事舉以為問。愚竊以謂，四君豈我聖祖之疇匹也哉？蓋高帝寬仁大度，光武同符高祖，太宗濟世安民，藝祖仁厚立國，固皆不嗜殺人者也。然而學識或未醇，充養或未至，故始雖能一天下，而至於立國詒謀，終不能以無議。比而同之，是以事物有形之粗而擬諸天地變化之神也。况我聖祖得天下之正，功高萬古，雖高光特近似焉，而豈唐宗宋祖所可得而彷彿之哉？彼四君者，無庸論矣。
嘗聞洪武中，臣下建白，每依忠厚。姑舉其一二，如王待制則曰：「上天以生物為心，人君體上天生物之心，故一動一靜之間，務合乎天。」桂彥良則曰：「天道好生，聖人亦好生。好生之德洽于人心，則人皆化於為善。」二臣之言既見嘉納，而御製《睿志》又有感于詹同刑不上大夫之奏
translation_en:
…the four rulers who unified All-under-Heaven, whom you have brought forward in your question. In my humble opinion, how could these four rulers rank alongside our Sagely Progenitor? Emperor Gao of Han was generous, humane, and magnanimous; Guangwu matched Gaozu in these qualities; Taizong of Tang delivered the age from distress and brought peace to the people; and Yizu, the founding emperor of Song, established his state through humanity and generosity. Certainly, none delighted in killing. Yet their learning and understanding were perhaps not wholly sound, or their moral cultivation had not reached perfection. Thus, although they could initially unify All-under-Heaven, their establishment of the state and their plans for posterity ultimately could not escape criticism. To compare them with our Sagely Progenitor and place them on an equal footing is to liken the crude, tangible forms of things to the wondrous transformations of Heaven and Earth. Moreover, our Sagely Progenitor acquired All-under-Heaven with perfect legitimacy, and his achievements surpassed those of all antiquity. Even Gaozu and Guangwu bore only a near resemblance to him. How could Taizong of Tang and Taizu of Song possibly approach him? There is no need to discuss those four rulers further.
I have heard that during the Hongwu reign, officials consistently grounded their proposals in loyalty and generosity. Let me cite just one or two examples. Auxiliary Academician Wang said: “Heaven takes the generation of living things as its purpose. The ruler embodies this life-giving purpose of Heaven; therefore, in every movement and every moment of repose, he must strive to accord with Heaven.” Gui Yanliang said: “The Way of Heaven cherishes life, and the sage likewise cherishes life. When the virtue of cherishing life permeates people’s hearts, all are transformed toward goodness.” The words of these two officials received gracious approval, while the imperially composed Sagely Aspirations (Ruizhi) was also inspired by Zhan Tong’s memorial arguing that punishments should not extend to grandees…

第二問
姚淶
同考試官主事薛批：朱陸之學，今其書具在。士之善學者，跡其同異而别其優劣，要自有定論。抑古人為學，不患夫辨同異優劣之難，而在夫躬行之難。然則今之君子，無乃後於躬行而嗜於言者與？子謂之曰多言，盖誠是也。且中間考析諸儒，亦自精確，可謂有識之士矣。
同考試官給事中夏批：諸儒皆有功吾道，朱子實有功諸儒。講學不免異同，而折衷其有定論。至於陸氏之學，要亦自得，有不必強合
translation_en:
…Thereupon he repeatedly exercised reverent concern in administering punishments, even having the instruments of punishment of the Embroidered Uniform Guard brought out and burned. Through fairness and forbearance he brought peace to the myriad people. This was already accomplished without waiting for an era of rulers preserving an established dynasty. Even in the canonical accounts of the Five Emperors and Three Kings, such deeds were perhaps unheard of. Ah, how magnificent! The Book of Documents says: “The sage has counsels and instructions; clearly verify them and thereby secure lasting protection.” This describes the Ancestral Injunctions. If you, sir, deem this worthy of being presented [?], I venture respectfully to offer it to His Majesty.
Second policy question
Yao Lai 姚淶
Comment by Associate Examiner Xue, Secretary: The writings concerning the learning of Zhu Xi and Lu Jiuyuan are all still extant. A scholar who knows how to learn can trace their agreements and differences and distinguish their relative merits; there must ultimately be a settled judgment. Yet for the ancients, the difficulty in learning lay less in distinguishing agreements, differences, and relative merits than in putting their learning into practice. Might not the gentlemen of today, then, neglect personal practice while delighting in words? You call this “much talk,” and that is indeed correct. Moreover, your examination and analysis of the various Confucian scholars in the body of the essay are precise. You may rightly be called a scholar of discernment.
Comment by Associate Examiner Xia, Supervising Secretary: The various Confucian scholars have all rendered service to our Way, and Master Zhu truly rendered service to those scholars. In discussing learning, agreements and differences are inevitable, but there is a settled judgment by which to adjudicate them. As for Master Lu’s learning, it too rests ultimately on insights he attained for himself; there are points that need not be forcibly reconciled…

title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
必求同偏詆以立異者此策考析詳明議論精
確蓋亦知所自擇而不惑於多言者邪
同考試官編修陳批史記作儒林傳後
因之宋史乃有道學傳以孟氏之學實續于宋
之諸儒而別于朱子立傳之意夫復何言此
策能析當時諸學之同異而歸于集大成者之
心雖有他說亦可以自破矣

集長之說以見朱子之心非善審其是而可與

translation_en:
…insisting on agreement, or disparaging others one-sidedly to establish differences. This policy essay offers detailed and clear analysis and precise argument. Surely its author also knows how to choose for himself without being confused by a profusion of words?

Associate Examiner Chen, a Hanlin Academy Compiler, comments: The Records of the Grand Historian established the “Biographies of Confucian Scholars,” and later histories followed it. The History of the Song, however, includes “Biographies of Masters of the Learning of the Way,” because the learning of Mengzi was truly carried on by the Confucian scholars of the Song. As for the intention behind giving Zhu Xi a separate biography, what more need be said? This policy essay can distinguish the similarities and differences among the various teachings of that time and arrive at the intent of the master who brought them together into a comprehensive whole. Even if there are other interpretations, they can thereby be refuted.

Associate Examiner Wang, a Hanlin Academy Compiler, comments: In teaching others, our Master took ease and simplicity as his guiding principles and put them into practice through broad learning and disciplined restraint. These are the standards for students of all ages. Yet Zhu Xi and Lu differed in their approaches to learning, each proceeding according to his own understanding; they could not agree in every respect. This was surely already true even among the seventy disciples in the Master’s own time. This policy essay invokes turning back to oneself and exerting effort, eliminating shortcomings and gathering strengths, to reveal Zhu Xi’s intent. Is its author not someone who discerns what is right and with whom one may pursue learning?

Associate Examiner □, a Hanlin Academy Senior Compiler, comments: During the Chunxi and Qingyuan reign periods, the learning of Cheng and Zhu was severely proscribed. Those with discernment already foresaw that the Song dynasty’s virtue would not endure. This policy essay analyzes the similarities and differences among the Confucian scholars with exceptional clarity. At its close, it speaks further of rectifying the foundations, an argument particularly capable of strengthening the vital force of the state. Surely its author has gained an understanding of Cheng and Zhu? Moreover, his policy essays are expansive and learned, and his work in the preceding sessions was also excellent. The final character 本 begins an incomplete phrase [?]…

text:

考試官大學士石批考訂諸儒異同精而
不刻而末復以體道衞道為說得孟子反經之
遺意尤為卓識

之明如日中天以嘉惠天下萬世後之人
亦惟誦其言以究其理宗其教以淑其身
斯已矣而何以多言為哉嗚呼吾道晦明
之機誠繋于□是不可以不審也謹承明

translation_en:
…the foremost of the imperial command [?]; surely the presiding examiners cannot pass you over.
Examiner and Grand Secretary Shi comments: Your examination of the agreements and differences among the Confucian scholars is precise without being overly exacting. At the end, you further discuss embodying and defending the Way, capturing the spirit of Mencius’s return to the constant norms. This shows especially outstanding discernment.
Examiner and Grand Secretary Shen comments: The five policy essays are powerful, full-bodied, elegant, and free-flowing, while their reasoning is precise and profound. Their insight [illegible and doubtful text]; the discourse and memorial are also commensurate in quality. To think that such an extraordinary scholar should be found in the examination hall!
How does the Way become clear? Great Confucian scholars make it so. How does it become obscured? Excessive talk throws it into confusion. Since sages ceased to arise, the great principles have long been distorted. Fortunately, great Confucian scholars have emerged, bringing partial and distorted views together and returning them to their source. They have made our Way shine like the sun at midday, bestowing blessings upon all under Heaven for countless generations. Those who come after need only recite their words to investigate their principles and follow their teachings to cultivate themselves. That is all; what need is there for excessive talk? Alas! Whether our Way is obscured or illuminated truly depends upon [illegible]. This must be carefully examined. Having respectfully received your illuminating question, I beg leave to reply.
The sages are distant and their words have fallen into obscurity; it has long been the case that people throughout the realm do not know how to learn. Scholars of the Han sought understanding through textual glosses, while those of the Tang were immersed in literary composition. By the Song, [illegible] great Confucian scholars emerged. As the saying goes: after Kongzi, Zengzi and Zisi carried on his subtle teachings, which only became manifest with Mengzi; after Mengzi…

title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
周程張子繼其絕至朱子而始著究極源
委誰為至論宋史創為道學傳載其言行
以垂法後世非有得於此歟說者曰元祐
道學之興廢係司馬光之存亡紹興道學
之興廢係趙鼎之用舍慶元道學之興廢
係趙汝愚之去留嗟乎道之將行也與命
也道之將廢也與命也而豈獨人謀之弗
臧哉政事學術之禁發於孔文仲而成於
蔡京專門曲說之禁發於陳公輔而成於
===
秦檜以孝宗之英明而惑於王淮之私說
偽學之禁始立以寧宗之昏庸而濟以韓
侂冑之奸回偽學之禁始嚴君子所為眾
人固不識也豈獨胡澹陳賈輩之可罪哉
朱子當其時雖遭嚴禁講學不輟惟曰孜
孜斃而後已上而帝王傳心之奧下而學
者入德之門發明融會殆無餘蘊夷攷其
同時諸儒尚經制而求合乎先王攷禮樂
以振起乎流俗若陳傅良者為東嘉之學

周程張子繼其絶恵求乎而始著究極源
委〔誤矣〕至論宋史創為道學傳載其言行
以垂法後世非有得於此歟說者曰元祜
道學之興廢係司馬光之存亡紹興道學
之興廢係趙鼎〔之〕用舍慶元道學之興廢
係趙汝愚之去留〔噫〕斯乎道之將行也與命
也道之將廢也與命也而豈獨人謀之弗
臧哉政事學術之禁發於孔文仲而成於
蔡京專門曲說之禁發於陳公輔而成於
===
秦檜以孝宗之英明而惑於王淮之私說
偽學之禁始立以寧宗之昏庸而濟以韓
侂胄之奸回偽學之禁始嚴君子所為衆
人固不識也〔豈〕擢〔用〕陳賈輩之可罪哉
〔□□〕當其時〔雖〕道廢禁講學不輟惟日孜
孜斃而後已上下帝王傳心之奥下而學
者入德之門發明融會殆無餘藴寔孜其
同時諸儒尚經制而求合乎先王攻禮樂
以振拔乎流俗若陳傅良者為東嘉之學
punctuated:
周程張子繼其絕，至朱子而始著。究極源委，誰為至論？宋史創為道學傳，載其言行，以垂法後世，非有得於此歟？說者曰：「元祐道學之興廢，係司馬光之存亡；紹興道學之興廢，係趙鼎之用舍；慶元道學之興廢，係趙汝愚之去留。」嗟乎！道之將行也與，命也；道之將廢也與，命也。而豈獨人謀之弗臧哉？政事學術之禁，發於孔文仲而成於蔡京；專門曲說之禁，發於陳公輔而成於秦檜。以孝宗之英明，而惑於王淮之私說，偽學之禁始立；以寧宗之昏庸，而濟以韓侂冑之奸回，偽學之禁始嚴。君子所為，眾人固不識也，豈獨胡澹陳賈輩之可罪哉？

朱子當其時，雖遭嚴禁，講學不輟，惟曰：「孜孜，斃而後已。」上而帝王傳心之奧，下而學者入德之門，發明融會，殆無餘蘊。夷攷其同時諸儒，尚經制而求合乎先王，攷禮樂以振起乎流俗，若陳傅良者，為東嘉之學。
translation_en:
…Masters Zhou, Cheng, and Zhang carried on the transmission after it had been broken, and only with Master Zhu did it become fully manifest. Tracing its origins and development to their utmost limits, whose account may be deemed definitive? The History of the Song established a new section, “Biographies of Masters of the Learning of the Way,” recording their words and deeds to provide models for later generations. Was this not because its compilers had grasped something of this? Commentators say: “During the Yuanyou era, the flourishing or suppression of the Learning of the Way depended on whether Sima Guang lived or died; during the Shaoxing era, on whether Zhao Ding was employed or set aside; and during the Qingyuan era, on whether Zhao Ruyu was dismissed or retained.” Alas! Whether the Way is to prevail is a matter of destiny; whether the Way is to be cast aside is a matter of destiny. Yet could this have been solely a matter of ill-conceived human designs? The prohibition concerning government affairs and scholarly learning originated with Kong Wenzhong and was brought to completion by Cai Jing; the prohibition against the distorted doctrines of a particular school originated with Chen Gongfu and was brought to completion by Qin Hui. Despite Emperor Xiaozong’s brilliance, he was misled by Wang Huai’s self-serving arguments, and the prohibition against “spurious learning” was first established. Emperor Ningzong’s benighted mediocrity, compounded by Han Tuozhou’s treachery and perversity, then made that prohibition severe. Ordinary people assuredly do not understand what gentlemen do. How could men such as Hu Dan and Chen Jia alone deserve blame?

In those days, although Master Zhu faced severe prohibitions, he did not cease teaching and discussing learning. He said only: “I shall labor diligently, stopping only at death.” From the profound mysteries of the transmission of the mind among emperors and kings above, to the gateway through which students enter into virtue below, he elucidated and integrated them, leaving scarcely any hidden meaning unexplored. If we impartially examine the other Confucian scholars of his time, those such as Chen Fuliang esteemed institutions of government and sought conformity with the former kings, investigating rites and music to rouse people above prevailing vulgar customs: theirs was the learning of Dongjia.

title: 嘉靖二年會試錄
text:
智數法術可以馭兵而料敵剛烈之氣足
以震威而翕張若陳亮者為永康之學夢
寐即白晝之為屋漏即康衢之見若陸九
淵兄弟者為金谿之學稽經以該物理訂
史以參事情若呂祖謙者為金華之學嚴
於義利之辨若張栻者為廣漢之學夫傅
良之學失之固亮之學失之豪無足言矣
祖謙精於稽古而得中原文献之傳栻銳
於希顏而有春風沂水之樂皆本濂洛之
===
正脉故與朱子鼎立而為三三子學同道
同而傳宋史者列敬夫於道學而伯恭不
與焉何哉盖造詣淺深之異也至于陸氏
之學則又異於□□矣盖其學專以先立
乎其大者為言非不致知也其所以致知
者異乎人之致知非不集義也其所以集
義者異乎人之集義朱陸之辨毫釐千里
正在於此太極一圖二程得於濂溪者也
顧謂非有太極圖言無極獨不思易之言

Chen Liang represented this learning of Yongkang. Conduct in dreams was the same as conduct in broad daylight; what was shown in the secluded corner of one's room was the same as what was shown on a public thoroughfare. Lu Jiuyuan and his brothers represented this learning of Jinxi. Examining the classics to comprehend the principles of things, and critically studying history to investigate the circumstances of affairs: Lü Zuqian represented this learning of Jinhua. Strict discrimination between righteousness and profit characterized Zhang Shi's learning of Guanghan.

Chen Fuliang's learning erred in rigidity, and Chen Liang's in boldness; they merit no further discussion. Zuqian excelled in investigating antiquity and inherited the textual and cultural traditions of the Central Plain. Zhang Shi eagerly aspired to emulate Yan Hui and enjoyed the delight of spring breezes and the Yi River. Both drew upon the orthodox lineage of Lianxi and Luoyang, and thus stood alongside Master Zhu as the three legs of a tripod. These three masters shared the same learning and the same Way. Yet those who compiled the biographies in the History of the Song placed Jingfu [Zhang Shi] among the exponents of Learning of the Way, while Bogong [Lü Zuqian] was not included. Why? Presumably because their attainments differed in depth.

As for the learning of the Lu family, it differed yet again from □□ [illegible]. Their teaching concentrated exclusively on the injunction to establish first the greater part of oneself. It was not that they failed to extend knowledge, but their means of extending knowledge differed from those of others. It was not that they failed to accumulate righteousness, but their means of accumulating righteousness differed from those of others. …the way of accomplishment, the Way of Heaven and Earth. His argument is brilliant and vigorous, its splendor compelling; his talent and discernment far surpass those of others.
Those who govern must first establish the fundamental substance of government and then adapt its application to circumstances; only thus can they attain government free of defects. That the realm remains ill-governed is not because its circumstances are inherently difficult. If one's understanding is unsettled, one's actions will inevitably be one-sided. To remedy that one-sidedness only after it has arisen means not merely that government is already corrupted, but that our efforts become all the more difficult. Moreover, among the matters on which order and disorder depend are some that cannot be handled hastily. How, then, could one fail to examine them? The [?] ruler proceeds otherwise: he carefully determines a settled method to uphold, while also weighing urgency against delay and assessing the relative gravity of matters, thereby making good its deficiencies. Thus laws are established without flaws, and affairs are carried through without contravening what is right. Is this not how emperors and kings governed from antiquity, and what later generations ought to emulate?
Now, the way of governing has long been difficult to expound. Those who esteem virtue invariably advocate leniency; yet leniency invariably lapses into indulgence, which is not the proper expression of virtue. Those who esteem law invariably advocate severity; yet severity invariably lapses into cruelty, which is not the proper expression of law. Confucius said: “When government is lenient, the people grow lax; when they grow lax, correct them with sternness. Sternness injures the people; when they are injured, relieve them with leniency.” Master Xu, known as Luzhai, called this an unchanging, constant Way. Yet I humbly believe these are not Confucius's words, but an error in the recording of rites [?]. For if leniency has already produced laxity before sternness is applied…

title: 嘉靖二年會試錄

孰若未慢之先知所以節之乎猛至於殘
而后寛行焉孰若未殘之先知所以制之
乎此一偏之説也且猛之為言豈為人父
母如其赤子者哉故愚以為非孔子之言
也記者之誤也不然則有為而發也請以

不本於身心閨門無禮輕儇見誚則經術
不行於妻子殆未知禮樂之本也不畏強

人似矣而簿書之累則有所不免殆未知
刑政之本也此其血氣用事隨世以就功

translation_en:
…how could that compare with knowing how to restrain them before they become unruly? When severity reaches the point of cruelty, leniency is then applied; how could that compare with knowing how to check it before cruelty arises? This is a one-sided view. Moreover, how could speaking of severity befit one who acts as the people's parent and treats them as his infant children? Thus I humbly believe these were not Confucius's words, but an error by the recorder. Otherwise, they must have been spoken in response to particular circumstances.

Let me turn to those of antiquity acclaimed for good government: no age surpassed the Han in capable officials. When Han Yanshou was in Yingchuan, he taught the people ritual propriety and deference and established ceremonial forms and distinctions; he may be said to have cherished antiquity and promoted moral instruction. When Zhao Guanghan was in Jingzhao, he acted with the swiftness of the wind upon perceiving a matter, shrinking from nothing; he may be said to have curbed the powerful and overbearing through his authority. Grounding his learning in the Spring and Autumn Annals and drawing on the Classic for support—such was Zhang Chang's administration in Jingzhao. Keeping registers of evildoers and, by dealing with one, warning a hundred [?]—such was Yin Wenggui's administration in Fufeng.

These four men were not without merits. Yet extravagance and presumption in carriages, attire, and guards [?], exceeding prescribed limits, showed that moral instruction was not rooted in one's own person and mind. A lack of ritual propriety within the household, drawing reproach for frivolous conduct, showed that classical learning was not put into practice among one's wife and children. They had perhaps not understood the foundations of rites and music. Not fearing the powerful and overbearing seems right, but probing and entrapping techniques were not appropriate means to employ. Consulting registers to apprehend people seems right, but this could not escape the encumbrances of paperwork. They had perhaps not understood the foundations of punishments and government. They merely let their passions govern their actions and followed the ways of their age to attain achievement and fame. How, then, could one expect them to understand gentleness and firmness, and to be able to apply them at the proper time…

punctuated:
之道也。於戲！進於此者希矣。孔子嘗以惠人稱子産，今考其相鄭之跡，如黜汰侈、明察辟、鑄刑書、作丘賦，則未嘗不嚴。其告子太叔曰：「唯有德能以寬服民，其次莫如猛。」盖有以識此矣。程子嘗以儒者許孔明，今考其治蜀之效，如賞不遺遠，罰不阿近，爵不可以無功取，刑不可以貴勢免，亦未嘗不嚴也。其言曰：「治世以大德，不以小惠。」盖有以知此矣。故子産以區區之鄭，變弱為强，晉楚大姓無敢梗其政；孔明以一隅之蜀，轉危為安，而吳魏竊視，不敢加以兵，非知治體者乎？雖然，乗輿濟人，知食而不知教；親校簿書，寫申韓以授後主，猶有未盡善焉者。
愚聞先王之政也，修六禮以節民性，明七教以興民德，齊八政以防淫，一道德以同俗，養耆老以致孝，恤孤獨以逮不足，上賢以崇德，簡不肖以絀惡。彼其法制禁令不可踰越，而仁愛之意未嘗不行
translation_en:
…the way of doing so. Alas! Few have advanced to this level. Confucius once called Zichan a benevolent man. Yet if we now examine his deeds as chief minister of Zheng—suppressing extravagance, scrutinizing penal laws, casting the penal code in bronze, and instituting the levy on land units called qiu—he was never without strictness. He told Zi Taishu: “Only those possessed of virtue can make the people submit through leniency; next to this, nothing is as effective as severity.” He evidently had some understanding of this principle. Master Cheng once recognized Kongming as a Confucian. Yet if we now examine the results of his government of Shu—rewards did not overlook those distant from him, punishments did not favor those close to him, rank could not be obtained without merit, and punishment could not be escaped through noble status or power—he too was never without strictness. He said: “Govern the world through great virtue, not through petty favors.” He evidently understood this principle. Thus Zichan transformed the tiny state of Zheng from weakness to strength, and neither Jin and Chu nor the great clans dared obstruct his government. Kongming turned the peril of Shu, confined to one corner of the realm, into security; Wu and Wei watched covertly but dared not attack. Were these not men who understood the essentials of government? Even so, ferrying people across in one's carriage, knowing how to feed them but not how to teach them; personally checking registers and documents, and copying the writings of Shen Buhai and Han Fei to give to the Later Ruler—these were still matters in which they fell short of complete excellence.
I have humbly heard that in their government the former kings cultivated the six rites to regulate the people's dispositions, clarified the seven teachings to promote the people's virtue, and ordered the eight functions of government to guard against excess. They unified moral principles to bring customs into accord, cared for the elderly to foster filial piety, relieved orphans and the solitary to reach those in need, elevated the worthy to honor virtue, and distinguished the unworthy to suppress evil. Their laws, institutions, prohibitions, and commands could not be transgressed, yet their benevolent and loving intentions never failed to find expression…

乎？其為政則粹乎無以議也。今天下之政弊矣，上下恬嬉，而苟且之文多；賦繁役重，而蠲貸之恩薄。細民無以安其生，大憝得以逭其罪。宜乎田野愁嘆者多，而閭閻遊食者未減也。為今之計，其惟本之以嚴，而濟之以寬乎？蓋禮法明，教化修，由是平易出之可也。今偷惰姑息，責實之效不聞，天下之勢日趨於弱，猶泄泄然以寬為事，夫豈先王之寬哉？故必精明其治功，振作其治體，有功必賞，有罪必罰，便民者必行，殃民者必去，使凡法度之施莫非實效。有所不及，則以寬濟之，庶乎其可也。蓋嚴，體也；寬，用也。先立其體，而後隨宜以為之用也。
然此非愚之言也。朱子曰：「為政當以嚴為本，而以寬濟之。」朱子嘗言之矣。亦非朱子之言也。《曲禮》曰：「莅官行法，非禮威嚴不行。」《曲禮》曾言之矣。亦非《曲禮》之言也。不專一則不能直遂，不翕聚則不能發散，天地之道
translation_en:
… did it not? Their government was so pure that there was nothing to criticize. Today, government throughout the realm has fallen into decay. Those above and below idle complacently, and makeshift formalities abound; taxes are numerous and labor obligations heavy, yet the grace of remission and relief is scant. Ordinary people have no means of securing their livelihoods, while great malefactors escape punishment. Little wonder that so many in the countryside lament in distress, while the number living idly in the towns has not diminished. For present purposes, should we not make strictness the foundation and temper it with leniency? Once rites and laws are clear and moral instruction is cultivated, it is permissible to administer government with ease and simplicity. Today, however, there is indolence and indulgence, and no evident success in demanding actual results. The realm grows weaker by the day, yet officials remain slack and make leniency their business. How could this be the leniency of the former kings? We must therefore bring discernment and clarity to the work of government and reinvigorate its governing framework. Those with merit must be rewarded, those guilty of offenses punished; measures beneficial to the people must be implemented, and those harmful to them abolished. Every application of laws and institutions must produce actual results. Where these fall short, temper them with leniency: then perhaps government will be sound. Strictness is the substance; leniency is its application. First establish the substance, and then adapt its application to circumstances.
Yet these are not my own humble words. Master Zhu said, “In governing, one should make strictness the foundation and temper it with leniency.” Master Zhu already said this. Nor did the saying originate with Master Zhu. The “Summary of the Rules of Propriety” (Quli) says, “In holding office and enforcing laws, without ritual propriety, authority and strictness cannot be exercised.” The Quli already said this. Nor did the principle originate with the Quli. Without concentration on one thing, there can be no direct advance; without gathering together, there can be no spreading outward. The Way of Heaven and Earth …

君子其可不慎哉且朋黨之說不聞於盛
