廢。立□，則其相與也必激；激則爭，爭則天下之私自此而基。廢公基私，其源雖微，其流則傾覆而不可拯，漢唐宋之朋黨是已。君子其可不慎哉？

且朋黨之說不聞於盛世者，何也？愚嘗觀諸《易》矣：泰以九二為中行，是臣道也。臣道得其中，則可以事上；上以志同而交於我，朋之亡者，蓋本諸包荒也。又嘗觀於《書》矣：洪範以五為皇極，是君道也。君道得其中，則可以使下；下以保極，而時無我朋之淫者，蓋化於大受也。上下交，則德業成。其同寅協恭以底于治，譬則韶章之奏，雖八音有無始終條理之異，而其雝雝和鳴則一，無不同也。初何有於朋黨哉？

漢□□□，故善類禁錮，而炎祚遂傾。然其始特□□客之相標榜而已，執事所謂甘陵分部是也。唐以朋黨之故，正人擯斥，而唐宗遂覆。然其始特私怨之相傾軋而已，執事所謂牛李爭權是也。覆轍在
translation_en:
…is abolished. When people set themselves apart [?], their dealings with one another inevitably become provocative; provocation leads to contention, and contention lays the foundation for selfish interests throughout the realm. Abolishing the public good and establishing private interests may begin imperceptibly, but the consequences bring an overthrow beyond remedy. Such were the factions of the Han, Tang, and Song. Can the gentleman fail to exercise caution?

Moreover, why do we not hear of factions in flourishing ages? I have considered this in the Book of Changes. In the hexagram Tai, the nine in the second place represents walking the middle course: this is the way of the minister. When the minister’s way attains its proper mean, he can serve his superior. His superior shares his purpose and enters into fellowship with him; the disappearance of partisan attachments is surely rooted in his capacity to embrace even the uncultivated. I have also considered this in the Book of Documents. In the “Great Plan,” the fifth category is the August Ultimate: this is the way of the ruler. When the ruler’s way attains its proper mean, he can direct his subordinates. His subordinates uphold the Ultimate, and there is then no excess of self-serving factionalism [?], because they have been transformed by his all-embracing reception of them. When superiors and subordinates enter into fellowship, virtue and achievement are brought to fruition. Their shared reverence and united respect, through which they attain good government, resemble the performance of the Shao music. Although the eight classes of instruments differ in when they sound or fall silent, and in the ordered sequence of their beginnings and endings, their harmonious resonance is one: none fails to accord. Where could factionalism arise in this?

Under the Han, [text illegible], worthy men were barred from office, and the dynasty’s fiery mandate consequently collapsed. Yet at the outset this was merely a matter of certain associates [?] promoting one another’s reputations: what you, honored examiner, call the division into camps at Ganling. Under the Tang, factionalism caused upright men to be excluded, and the Tang ruling house consequently fell. Yet at the outset this was merely a matter of people undermining one another out of private resentment: what you call the struggle for power between Niu and Li. The tracks of these overturned carriages lie…

…before them, yet □□ took no warning [?]. There is something still more deserving of criticism. When Sima Guang sought to rescue the government [?], he reversed everything Wang Anshi had done, and the faction of petty men was consequently expelled. When Zhang Dun and Lü Huiqing were again employed [?], they reversed everything Sima Guang and Lü Dafang had done, and the faction of gentlemen was consequently extinguished. This went far beyond Lü Yijian’s jealousy of Fan Zhongyan and his □□□□ treatment of him [?]. What brought this about began with Yang Wei’s □□□ concerning Dafang [?], followed by Li Qingchen’s mediation in securing advancement. The purpose behind supporting this course was to have Emperor Zhezong carry on the New Policies implemented during the Xining reign period. Those men used this opportunity to indulge their private desire for revenge. In the end, all the gentlemen were driven out, the ranks of the wicked grew daily, and the people of the realm once more suffered grievous torment. As a result, the Song court crossed south of the Yangzi.
Alas! How terrible and fearsome are the calamities caused by factions! Public-mindedness is extinguished by private interests, and calamity arises from excessive provocation. Fan Chunren evidently understood this. When Lü Huiqing and his associates were first expelled, he advised: “One should not scrutinize people’s faults too harshly.” When Cai Que and his associates were expelled, he again □□□ that people should not be condemned for their spoken or written words [?]. His planning for the state was indeed far-sighted; Wen commends him for this [?]. Yet the upright could not prevail over the wicked, the affairs of state fell into decline, and Chunren too was expelled. Even a wise man could hardly have set matters right afterward!
Well said were Ouyang Xiu’s words: “Gentlemen have indeed generally been few, while petty □□ seek out those of their kind and remove them all [?], merely labeling them a faction…”
